read-the-fold-receipt.text: The first individually foldable request for a key keeps it in take order. An earlier unfoldable request never reserves the key. If every discovered holder is skipped, nothing to fold still carries every skipped reference and reason.

read-the-measured-limits.name: docs-folding-requests/read-the-measured-limits-01
read-the-measured-limits.text: These are evaluations of kept transactions under the preprod parameters recorded on 4 October 2026 in offchain/test/fixtures/koios/preprod/cli_protocol_params-b777448425778d13.json. A development node given the same limits, prices and fees corroborates the accepted size and refusal of the next. This is not a submission to preprod. The packaged node cannot run preprod's current execution model; the ledger evaluator uses the recorded target model separately. Protocol parameters can change by governance.

read-the-measured-limits.name: docs-folding-requests/read-the-measured-limits-02
read-the-measured-limits.text: The transaction slots use the captured development network's time. The result is script evaluation under the recorded parameters, not preprod transaction validation or inclusion. The fees are those of the kept node-balanced bodies, not a quote for another network. Re-evaluating the same kept bytes reproduces the figures; fresh captures may vary and publish their differences separately.

read-the-measured-limits.name: docs-folding-requests/read-the-measured-limits-03
read-the-measured-limits.text: These figures are generated from the kept measurement receipt.

read-the-measured-limits.name: docs-folding-requests/read-the-measured-limits-04
read-the-measured-limits.text: The largest accepted named prefix and the next refused size follow. Bytes are the complete signed transaction length; ledger-counted bytes are listed separately. Fees are lovelace from the development-node-balanced transaction body.

read-the-measured-limits.name: docs-folding-requests/read-the-measured-limits-05
read-the-measured-limits.text: Per-request figures are exact total divided by accepted count, including transaction overhead. A fraction is exact, not a rounded price.

read-the-measured-limits.name: docs-folding-requests/read-the-measured-limits-06
read-the-measured-limits.text: The marginal last request is the difference from the preceding kept prefix. It is an observation for this ordered workload, not a constant cost per request.

read-the-measured-limits.name: docs-folding-requests/read-the-measured-limits-07
read-the-measured-limits.text: The workload starts from the registry sizes below. The listed sequence is the accepted named prefix; the mixed result concerns that alternating order only. The digest binds the full initial datum shapes in the receipt, alongside the kept trie inputs.

what-has-been-exercised.name: docs-folding-requests/what-has-been-exercised-01
what-has-been-exercised.text: The packaged development-network registration journey starts a folder in fresh directories with none of the booker's files. It discovers and folds a mixed batch, checks the folder's change from the chain, and accounts separately for folded, skipped and left requests. It skips another registry's request, the application's configuration holder that its request decoding does not accept, and an unfoldable duplicate. A duplicate-free control and a later fold of what was left accompany it.

what-has-been-exercised.name: docs-folding-requests/what-has-been-exercised-02
what-has-been-exercised.text: An approval at a key address and a malformed request datum are unit-tested only; the packaged journey does not construct accepted transactions creating those holders. Unit tests also exercise the other individually unfoldable reasons beside passing controls. Development-network refusals exercise a foreign named request, a duplicate key, an oversized named batch and a transaction moving another state-policy asset, each beside an accepted control. These observations do not establish an executable comparison with the model. The conformance record keeps those gaps visible.

what-the-measurement-does-not-cover.name: docs-folding-requests/what-the-measurement-does-not-cover-00
what-the-measurement-does-not-cover.text: What the measurement does not cover.

what-the-measurement-does-not-cover.name: docs-folding-requests/what-the-measurement-does-not-cover-01
what-the-measurement-does-not-cover.text: The figures concern exactly the registry sizes, trie inputs, scripts, keys, payload shapes and parameters in the receipt. They say nothing about another registry size, trie depth, scripts, key or payload shapes, or parameters. The mixed figure does not cover every ordering or every ratio of registrations to terminations. The trie library's proofs are assumed sound.

what-the-measurement-does-not-cover.name: docs-folding-requests/what-the-measurement-does-not-cover-02
what-the-measurement-does-not-cover.text: The command reference gives the surrounding registration and termination commands. The provider and wallet settings describe the options shared by the examples above.

how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.name: docs-install/how-a-release-gets-its-bundles-00
how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.text: How a release gets its bundles.

how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.name: docs-install/how-a-release-gets-its-bundles-01
how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.text: As a maintainer, you want a release to publish only bundles that were already built and run on their own platform, so that a broken platform is found in a pull request and never after the tag.

how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.name: docs-install/how-a-release-gets-its-bundles-02
how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.text: The Linux bundle is built on the self-hosted runner and the macOS bundle on a GitHub-hosted Apple Silicon runner, each from the release-bundle output of the repository's flake. A bundle failing on either platform fails the release before anything is published, and the publisher refuses a release that lacks a bundle for any platform listed in tools/release_bundles.sh. Nothing in a pull request publishes: the built tarballs are kept as workflow artifacts for a week.

how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.name: docs-install/how-a-release-gets-its-bundles-03
how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.text: The Linux packages and the Homebrew formula follow the organisation's shared release actions and Nix helpers (dev-assets). A pull request builds the AppImages, the DEB and the RPM, runs every command from each one unpacked, and then installs the DEB on Ubuntu and the RPM on Fedora and runs each AppImage, on machines without Nix. It also builds the formula from the macOS tarball, installs it through a local tap that points at that tarball, and runs brew test. The release tag publishes the Linux packages once the release exists. The formula follows once verify-release has passed: it is pushed to the organisation's tap only if the release's macOS tarball is the one the formula names, then installed from the tap and tested. A manual run of the bundles workflow can publish the dev channels: the dev-linux packages and the singular-dev formula.

how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.name: docs-install/how-a-release-gets-its-bundles-04
how-a-release-gets-its-bundles.text: A pull request that builds the bundles also plays the registration journey from those files, twice: from the Linux bundle unpacked, and from the DEB installed with the system package manager, each on a machine that has no Nix. The commands and the blueprint come only from the bundle or the package, and the development node is the one the bundle or the package carries; the job shows where each command and the blueprint resolved to. The journey creates a registry, registers, updates and terminates a key, reads it back and folds a discovered batch on a development network. Every verdict is computed from the chain's record or from files, and none is typed; create, register, update, terminate, read and the discovered batch fold are each judged from the chain's record and shown failing on altered input. The same pull request assembles the release as the pipeline does, adds both bundles and runs verify-release on it, so that a broken bundle journey is found in the pull request and not after the tag.

install-on-linux.name: docs-install/install-on-linux-01
install-on-linux.text: You need curl, tar and sha256sum, which every distribution carries. The programs bring their own C library and do not use the distribution's.

install-on-macos.name: docs-install/install-on-macos-01
install-on-macos.text: macOS ships curl, tar and shasum. The command is the same with the platform and the checksum tool changed.

install-on-macos.name: docs-install/install-on-macos-02
install-on-macos.text: The programs are signed ad hoc, which Apple Silicon requires of any program, and are not signed with an Apple developer certificate or notarised. A file downloaded with curl and unpacked with tar is not quarantined and runs. A file downloaded with a browser is quarantined, and macOS may refuse to open the programs inside it with a message that the developer cannot be verified. After you have checked the checksum, remove the quarantine mark once:

install-the-commands-without-nix.name: docs-install/install-the-commands-without-nix-01
install-the-commands-without-nix.text: You develop for Cardano on Linux or on an Apple Silicon Mac and you want to play the first demo without installing Nix or compiling the Haskell stack. On a Mac you install the commands with one Homebrew command; on Linux you install a DEB or an RPM, or run an AppImage; on either you can instead download the tarball for your platform, check it against the release's checksums and unpack it. You run singular --version and see the release and the commit the program was built from, and then run the commands of the first demo. From the release after 0.13.1 every one of these also holds the private development node the first demo starts, so that node needs no nix command either.

install-the-linux-packages.name: docs-install/install-the-linux-packages-01
install-the-linux-packages.text: For the releases after 0.13.1, a DEB or an RPM installs all three commands into /usr/bin, with everything they need, on any distribution of its family, and your package manager removes them again. An AppImage holds one command as one file you run where it lies.

install-the-linux-packages.name: docs-install/install-the-linux-packages-02
install-the-linux-packages.text: On Fedora and its relatives the RPM goes in the same way, with sudo dnf install ./singular-${version}-x86_64-linux.rpm. An AppImage, for example singular-${version}-x86_64-linux.AppImage, is made executable with chmod +x and run as ./singular-${version}-x86_64-linux.AppImage --version; it needs FUSE and user namespaces, which desktop distributions allow. The packages put their files under /nix/store and the commands in /usr/bin; they do not need Nix and do not install it.

install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac.name: docs-install/install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac-00
install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac.text: Install with Homebrew on a Mac.

install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac.name: docs-install/install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac-01
install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac.text: For the releases after 0.13.1, a Mac with Apple Silicon and Homebrew installs the latest release with one command, and brew upgrade takes the next one:

install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac.name: docs-install/install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac-02
install-with-homebrew-on-a-mac.text: Homebrew downloads the macOS tarball from the release, checks it against the checksum the formula carries and links singular, open-datum and devnet onto your path. The Cardano node stays inside the installation, where devnet finds it, so it never replaces a node you installed yourself. The formula's own test runs --version of the three commands.

other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.name: docs-install/other-platforms-and-the-nix-route-00
other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.text: Other platforms and the Nix route.

other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.name: docs-install/other-platforms-and-the-nix-route-01
other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.text: Releases carry bundles for Linux on x86_64 and macOS on Apple Silicon only. Linux on aarch64 and macOS on Intel have no bundle yet. On those, and for anyone who prefers it, the Nix route stays as it was: with Nix and flakes enabled, run a command straight from the release.

other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.name: docs-install/other-platforms-and-the-nix-route-02
other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.text: Both print the same release and commit line as the bundle's commands do.

other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.name: docs-install/other-platforms-and-the-nix-route-03
other-platforms-and-the-nix-route.text: To check a release end to end, including the commands built from its archive, follow Download and verify a release. That verifier also checks each bundle against the commit the release tag names.

what-is-inside-the-tarball.name: docs-install/what-is-inside-the-tarball-01
what-is-inside-the-tarball.text: The folder bin holds the commands you run: singular, open-datum, devnet and cardano-node. Each is a short launcher that points the real program at the libraries and data files in the same folder and starts it, so nothing is read from outside the folder, and moving the folder moves the installation.

what-is-inside-the-tarball.name: docs-install/what-is-inside-the-tarball-02
what-is-inside-the-tarball.text: The folder share also holds the deployment blueprint, plutus.json, that the commands take as --blueprint, with version.txt beside it naming the release: the on-chain archive carries the same blueprint and adjacent version label.

what-is-inside-the-tarball.name: docs-install/what-is-inside-the-tarball-03
what-is-inside-the-tarball.text: On Linux the folders lib and lib-node each also hold a C library and its loader, and the launcher starts the program through that loader, which is why the programs do not depend on the distribution's libraries. The Cardano node is built against another C library than the other three programs, which is why it has a folder of its own. On macOS the programs load only the libraries macOS itself provides and the ones in lib and lib-node.

what-you-download.name: docs-install/what-you-download-01
what-you-download.text: Every release after 0.12.0 carries one tarball per platform beside the documentation and on-chain archives, and one SHA256SUMS that lists all of them. A tarball holds both commands, singular and open-datum, with every library and data file they need. The tarballs of the releases after 0.13.1 also hold devnet, the program that starts a private development node, the Cardano node 10.7.0 it starts and the genesis files that node reads.

what-you-download.name: docs-install/what-you-download-02
what-you-download.text: The releases after 0.13.1 also carry the Linux packages, with their own checksum file singular-X.Y.Z-x86_64-linux.SHA256SUMS, and a Homebrew formula for the Mac. The sizes are approximate.

what-you-download.name: docs-install/what-you-download-03
what-you-download.text: Replace X.Y.Z with the release you want. The releases are listed at https://github.com/lambdasistemi/singular/releases.

what-you-see-when-it-works.name: docs-install/what-you-see-when-it-works-00
what-you-see-when-it-works.text: What you see when it works.

what-you-see-when-it-works.name: docs-install/what-you-see-when-it-works-01
what-you-see-when-it-works.text: Each command prints its name, the release and the commit it was built from, and exits with status 0. The commit is the one the release's tag names.

what-you-see-when-it-works.name: docs-install/what-you-see-when-it-works-02
what-you-see-when-it-works.text: The wallet commands run offline, so they are the quickest check that the programs work on your machine. Choose a passphrase; the program reads it from the standard input here and never takes it as an argument.

what-you-see-when-it-works.name: docs-install/what-you-see-when-it-works-03
what-you-see-when-it-works.text: Both commands print the same address, which begins with addr_test1 on the preprod network. From here the commands are the ones of the Demo 1.

what-you-see-when-it-works.name: docs-install/what-you-see-when-it-works-04
what-you-see-when-it-works.text: The development node starts with devnet and prints one line of settings once its chain is up. It runs until you stop it, and stopping devnet stops the Cardano node it started.

what-you-see-when-it-works.name: docs-install/what-you-see-when-it-works-05
what-you-see-when-it-works.text: The line is a JSON document that names the node's providerUrl and networkMagic, which is 42. The Demo 1 runbook in the singular-demo repository funds wallets on such a node and plays the whole demo. The node keeps its files in one folder under your temporary directory, so run one development node at a time.

where-the-blueprint-is.name: docs-install/where-the-blueprint-is-01
where-the-blueprint-is.text: Homebrew, the DEB, the RPM and the tarballs of a release after 0.13.1 bring the deployment blueprint the commands were released with, so Demo 1 needs no second download. It is the same file the on-chain archive ships as onchain/plutus.json, and verify-release checks that the two are identical. Each copy has the release's version.txt beside it.

where-the-blueprint-is.name: docs-install/where-the-blueprint-is-02
where-the-blueprint-is.text: Name it once and pass it to every command, for example blueprint=/usr/share/singular/plutus.json and then --blueprint "$blueprint".

how-to-change-effect-code.name: docs-io-ownership/how-to-change-effect-code-01

which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.name: docs-io-ownership/which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-recorded-00
which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.text: Which effects are gated, and which only recorded.

which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.name: docs-io-ownership/which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-recorded-01
which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.text: A gated effect needs a file-level entry in the ownership allowlist naming its owner, lifetime, access model and reason. A new file naming one without an entry fails; an entry whose effect is gone fails as stale.

which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.name: docs-io-ownership/which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-recorded-02
which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.text: Three rows deserve emphasis. No module imports the unsafe IO library, so no unsafe escape exists in the tree; the control that plants one proves the check rejects it. No module calls forkIO; the product's only concurrency is the Async library's scoped combinators. No module uses STM; the one match for the word is a theorem name, not a transaction, which is why the STM class is import-anchored rather than token-anchored.

which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.name: docs-io-ownership/which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-recorded-03
which-effects-are-gated-and-which-only-r.text: Two further surfaces are recorded by the census but enforced elsewhere. Timeout bounds belong to the calling-thread confirmation design, whose deadline tests own them. Environment reads belong to the explicit-input rule, whose release-build exclusion the release controls own. Their carriers are named in the evidence map below.

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-io-ownership/which-way-dependencies-run-01
which-way-dependencies-run.text: Effects flow one way: libraries expose capabilities, commands and runners compose them, tests drive them. Five boundaries hold this shape over the discovered extent — namespaces, not file lists, so a moved module is rechecked with nothing to edit:

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-io-ownership/which-way-dependencies-run-02
which-way-dependencies-run.text: the conformance library never imports the runner (the library stays runnable without live effects);

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-io-ownership/which-way-dependencies-run-03
which-way-dependencies-run.text: the offchain libraries never import the command layer (commands consume the libraries, never the reverse);

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-io-ownership/which-way-dependencies-run-04
which-way-dependencies-run.text: each journey executable keeps its local modules (old runners are never extended by sharing);

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-io-ownership/which-way-dependencies-run-05
which-way-dependencies-run.text: no ordinary executable links a host module (the adversary stays outside the release, its test-only reader excepted);

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-io-ownership/which-way-dependencies-run-06
which-way-dependencies-run.text: the command layer is imported only at composition — commands, applications and tests.

who-owns-an-effect.name: docs-io-ownership/who-owns-an-effect-01
who-owns-an-effect.text: A contributor adding a mutable cell, a worker thread or an environment read wants to know where it belongs, who releases it and what check will ask about it. A reviewer wants to see each effect's owner, lifetime and reason in one place instead of reconstructing them from imports. This page is that map: what the census covers, which effects are allowed where, which way the module boundaries run, what evidence backs each predecessor ticket, and what stays openly unfulfilled.

why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.name: docs-io-ownership/why-the-product-stays-single-threaded-01
why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.text: The product runs on the calling thread unless a written, compelling reason says otherwise, and no thread outlives the command that started it. Four sites carry such reasons, each beside its implementation with its join:

why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.name: docs-io-ownership/why-the-product-stays-single-threaded-02
why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.text: The devnet probe runs a node and a client together, joined before the probe returns.

why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.name: docs-io-ownership/why-the-product-stays-single-threaded-03
why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.text: The private facade serves sessions beside their followers, each session cancelling and joining its children before the next starts.

why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.name: docs-io-ownership/why-the-product-stays-single-threaded-04
why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.text: The conformance node runner holds one node-to-client thread per session, joined before the session ends.

why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.name: docs-io-ownership/why-the-product-stays-single-threaded-05
why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.text: The CLI-backend control bounds one confirmation wait with an explicit cancel, observed and joined before the run ends.

why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.name: docs-io-ownership/why-the-product-stays-single-threaded-06
why-the-product-stays-single-threaded.text: The test parallelism (two mapConcurrently_ shards over independent examples) and the test coordinations (entered/released/hold flags joined by withAsync before each example ends) are harness-owned: they run only under the suites, never in a release build. A newly introduced forkIO, async or concurrently site in a product package fails the ownership check until it is classified with its reason and its join.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-00
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: A worked example: resolving a registry before showing it.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-01
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: As a third-party reader built on this library, I am handed the address of a registry and want to show what it holds. A registry's datum pins four policies, and a genuine registry can pin policies its creator chose, so what I read from the datum means nothing until I have compared the pins with the ones the application derives. Singular.Registry.StateToken.resolveRegistry is that comparison. It takes the application, the release the registry was created under, the state token and one view of the chain, and gives back either the registry, whose datum has passed every check, or the refusal that names the first thing that does not.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-02
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: Over Mallory's registry, whose datum pins an active policy of her own, the function never reaches the first branch and the program prints:

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-03
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: The application you pass decides which pins are compared. An application that knows its own script, whether it states it as a blueprint title applied to the registry, as a compiled script or as a hash, has its application policy compared as well as the active witness policy. The neutral value used above knows none, so it takes the application policy from the datum, compares the active policy, and records that in the resolved registry: resolvedApplicationPin says whether the application policy was compared or was not checked against any blueprint, and a reader that shows registry content says so. A program that derives several applications from one registry, as open-datum does for its open and its closed registries, calls resolveRegistryAmong with its candidates and gets back the registry and the candidate the datum's application policy selects. pinsDifference is the comparison itself, exported for a command that creates a registry and wants to compare the datum it reads back with the pins it built.

a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-before-showing-it-04
a-worked-example-resolving-a-registry-be.text: The comparison is made when the registry is resolved and not again within the same run, because every fold preserves the pinned policies on chain; the protocol page says why a reader must make it.

appendix-discovered-adapter-consumers.text: This source inventory explains ownership, not ledger coverage. Each retained owner below uses serial access for the stated lifetime. how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-01
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: The reference cannot drift from the code it claims to document. The site build derives a manifest from the same off-chain source input Haddock ran on: for every module it records the digest of the Haskell source file and the digest of the actual generated source page. The site check then redoes both halves independently from this repository's own source tree — the manifest's module extent must equal the Cabal library extent, each recorded source digest must match the repository's file, and each generated page in the shipped site must match its recorded digest. A reference generated from any other source, however its label reads, fails that comparison; a page edited after generation fails its own digest.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-02
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: Every link inside the generated pages is inspected too. A reference from one module of this library to another — a type, a function, a module, however the tool that generated it spelled it — must resolve to a page of this reference and, where it names an anchor, to an anchor that exists. The check prints how many same-library links it resolved, and the reference's own index and guide links are checked by the site's ordinary link inventory.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-03
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: Dependency documentation is a different matter. The library is built against a large Cardano and Plutus dependency closure, and none of those packages' Haddock pages are bundled into this site: a type such as a ledger address or a Plutus core data value appears in the generated pages as a visible label, but it is not a link — following it would leave this site for documentation that is not shipped with it. Neutralizing those labels is decided from the build's own package database, which positively names every module each dependency owns, so a label is only unlinked when it provably belongs to a dependency; a dead or store-path link that reappears fails the site check, and a same-library reference may never be treated as a dependency label to hide a broken link.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-04
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: One further generator class is unlinked by structure. Haddock renders instance method names in each instance's Methods list as same-page links, but emits no matching anchors for them — every instance of a class lists the same method names, so the anchor would have to be duplicated. Those method labels stay visible as plain text inside the instance lists, and the site check both counts them separately and still requires every fragment link outside that exact structure to resolve.

how-the-reference-stays-honest.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/how-the-reference-stays-honest-05
how-the-reference-stays-honest.text: The release archive check extends the same discipline to what gets shipped: the staged documentation archive must carry the generated reference member for member and byte for byte before the ordinary release checks run.

interruptible-confirmation.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/interruptible-confirmation-01
interruptible-confirmation.text: An application author supplying registry capabilities wants a cancelled or expired command to stop its confirmation wait while retaining the transaction it already submitted. Registry commands and open-datum writes call capConfirm on the command's calling thread under the confirmation deadline. The callback confirms exactly the supplied signed transaction; it does not submit it again or start a background confirmation worker.

interruptible-confirmation.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/interruptible-confirmation-02
interruptible-confirmation.text: The command owns the wait and its cleanup. An IO callback must be interruptible through its transport reads, polling and resource cleanup, and must propagate asynchronous exceptions. A replacement that holds an uninterruptible block delays both deadline return and caller cancellation until that block releases. That is a capability limitation: it does not create a worker that can escape the command. Test harnesses observing this limit must release their barrier and join their command.

interruptible-confirmation.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/interruptible-confirmation-03
interruptible-confirmation.text: After acceptance by the submission endpoint, confirmation failure or deadline expiry leaves the signed identity journalled as unconfirmed. Caller cancellation also preserves that unresolved identity before propagating the original interruption. A provider failure is partial evidence, a deadline is a timeout, and neither is a ledger refusal or permission to resubmit. Success records confirmation; the command's independent readback remains a later step. The final receipt boundary rethrows asynchronous interruptions and a concrete WaitFailure unchanged: an infrastructure wait failure supplies no verdict and does not become a client or ledger refusal. Ordinary synchronous command failures and fallback receipts retain their existing classification. The module and field contract are in Singular.Registry.Capabilities. This effect contract leaves Lean's transaction law and the public capability signature unchanged.

off-chain-api-reference.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/off-chain-api-reference-01
off-chain-api-reference.text: A contributor reading the builder and blueprint guide wants to click a module of this library and land on its real interface — signatures, documentation, and the highlighted source — for exactly the code this repository ships. This page is the entry point of that reference for the off-chain registry library: a generated Haddock reference, rebuilt with the documentation site from this same source tree, so what you read here documents exactly the code this candidate was built from — and, as the extent below states, a few of its modules are documented for the contributor without being importable by a caller. One boundary on that promise is named below: identifiers and modules that belong to other packages are visible in the generated pages but are not clickable, because their documentation is not bundled with this site.

snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compatibility-01
snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.text: As a library consumer, you can compute a root, membership or exclusion proof, or an authenticated leaf from an MPF database value without allocating a mutable manager. The computation uses the existing MPF core and never treats the uncommitted key index as evidence for a leaf. A foreign observed root refuses authentication; inconsistent nodes prove no leaf. Malformed node decoding can still raise an exception, so the caller owns its evaluation and exception boundary.

snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compatibility-02
snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.text: The legacy names mkPureTrie, mkPureTrieFromRef, mkPureTrieManager and mkPureTrieManagerFrom identify the in-memory backend. Their IO adapters remain mutable. A caller owns the adapter and any dump action for the entire serial builder, replay or mirror lifetime. There is no locking or thread-safety guarantee. Sharing requires external serialization of complete sessions, including reads, writes, speculative snapshots, visibility changes and dumps. A dump includes hidden tries and is not an atomic concurrent snapshot. Missing and hidden manager lookups retain their existing exceptions, Trie not found: and Trie is hidden: followed by the shown token. Speculative sessions execute the existing pure stateTrie over a snapshot and discard the resulting database, without allocating a mutable copy. Action and mutation failures still occur during the IO callback; the returned value stays lazy, as it did with the mutable callback.

snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compatibility-03
snapshot-computations-and-mutable-compat.text: Ordinary registry and open-datum commands already authenticate through TrieState; the direct executable callers of the older CLI.Proof snapshot functions are the preservation tests. Removing their allocation alone is therefore a library computation improvement, not a claim that command session ownership changed.

what-the-reference-does-not-claim.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/what-the-reference-does-not-claim-01
what-the-reference-does-not-claim.text: This reference covers the off-chain registry library only. The four registry commands — the journey, insert-active, update-terminal and deployment — are executables, not library modules: their command-local modules are documented with source links in Who owns a registry command, and the library interfaces they call are the ones listed above. The conformance suite's own library now has its own generated reference — the Conformance API reference — generated and checked by the same discipline from the Conformance tree. Together the two references cover the documented module surfaces of the two public libraries, no more: this reference's extent is the off-chain main library's, with the runtime service modules staying outside it in Runtime service ownership, and the conformance reference's extent is the conformance library's. The executables and the on-chain Aiken validators remain outside the generated references. The public local-services component also exposes LocalEvaluation, NetworkTime, ProviderSettings, ProviderTrace, SessionEvidence, SessionIO, SessionServices, TimeSource, Trace, TraceRender, WaitTypes and Wallet; their sources live under offchain/local-services/Singular/Registry/. Their generated pages are not in this main-library reference. The public open-datum-application component (applications/open-datum/offchain/) carries the open-datum application the command line composes — command groups, envelope and release rules — and the request builders of the registry on the proved design: the booking of a registration, its reclaim by the refund address and its cleanup after the window, the configuration record added to the creation of a registry, the records and actions of the request validator in the layout it decodes, the validator as a transaction carries it, the reasons a builder declines, what open datum hands the fold of a registry, and the commands that create a registry and book, reclaim and clean up a registration: Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Build, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Command, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Envelope, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Registration, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Booking, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Configuration, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Fold, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Pending, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Records, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Refusal, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Requests.Script, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Root, Singular.Application.OpenDatum.Run; their sources live under applications/open-datum/offchain/src/Singular/Application/OpenDatum/, and the executable's entry point lives in applications/open-datum/offchain/app/. The public registry-cli component (offchain/cli/) carries the registry command line the two binaries link — session, journal and receipts, the flag group, registry helpers, reconciliation, recovery and the creation of a registry on the proved design with the fold into it: Singular.CLI, Singular.CLI.Command, Singular.CLI.Finish, Singular.CLI.Key, Singular.CLI.Live, Singular.CLI.ManagedState, Singular.CLI.Outlay, Singular.CLI.Payload, Singular.CLI.Plan, Singular.CLI.Promise, Singular.CLI.Proof, Singular.CLI.Receipt, Singular.CLI.ReceiptBody, Singular.CLI.Reconcile, Singular.CLI.Recovery, Singular.CLI.Registry, Singular.CLI.Root, Singular.CLI.Session, Singular.CLI.State, Singular.CLI.Steps, Singular.CLI.Trace, Singular.CLI.TrieTrace; their sources live under offchain/cli/src/Singular/CLI/.

what-this-reference-contains.text: The module extent is the public library of the off-chain Cabal file — every exposed module, every internal module, and every module the library re-exports under its own name. The module extent is discovered from the Cabal manifest. Explicitly exposed and re-exported modules are what a caller imports; the two trie capability owners behind the TrieState facade (Singular.Registry.TrieState.Core and .Types), the five wire owners behind the Types facade — Singular.Registry.Wire.Primitive, .Request, .State, .Proof and .Redeemer — and the three deployment owners behind the Deployment facade — Singular.Registry.Deployment.Manifest, .Mirror and .Attach — are package-internal other-modules with generated pages here for the contributor reading the facades' implementations, but no caller import path: a caller compiles against the facades' exports, not against these modules. The generic provider interface and evidence types let a caller supply capabilities without selecting a node runtime; the Koios constructor supplies unbound, unverified HTTP facts through that interface. The runtime service modules outside this extent — the terminal composition and its transport in koios-http, and the remaining service modules of local-services — are documented with source links in Runtime service ownership.
