what-this-reference-contains.name: docs-offchain-api-reference/what-this-reference-contains-04
what-this-reference-contains.text: The facades and owners of the registry builder and blueprint extraction are described module by module in the builder and blueprint modules guide, and the registry wire's five owners behind the Types facade in Who owns the registry wire.

behavioral-authority.name: docs-offchain-builder-blueprint/behavioral-authority-01
behavioral-authority.text: The registry conditions and application rules are the current model sources for these construction paths. The documentation ships those source files and checks their bytes against the candidate source. Changing or omitting a linked model artifact is rejected by the same check. Model statements, compiled-validator tests and connected journeys establish different boundaries; none substitutes for the others.

current-construction-paths.name: docs-offchain-builder-blueprint/current-construction-paths-01
current-construction-paths.text: The registry library owns creation, public state history, folds and reference publications. The application owns booking, holding updates, termination booking and registration exits. Commands resolve explicit inputs and submit the transactions these owners return. See fold responsibilities for the boundary between application request rules and registry state changes.

registry-builder-and-blueprint-modules.name: docs-offchain-builder-blueprint/registry-builder-and-blueprint-modules-01
registry-builder-and-blueprint-modules.text: As a contributor changing transaction construction, you want to find the current owner. Registry state and application requests have separate owners, and both use shared ledger providers and transaction assembly tools.

shared-representations.name: docs-offchain-builder-blueprint/shared-representations-01
shared-representations.text: The blueprint facade parses the CIP-57 schema, selects compiled code and applies parameters. Its Schema, Load and Params modules own those concerns separately. Shared internal helpers supply ledger-data conversions, script identity, lookup and balancing for retained callers. Funding and publication arithmetic remain shared with the preview so preview and construction use the same values.

shared-representations.name: docs-offchain-builder-blueprint/shared-representations-02
shared-representations.text: The API reference lists the discovered modules and links their signatures and source. Compilation establishes that the retained tree builds. Component tests and packaged journeys establish behavior at their respective boundaries; neither implies hosted CI or public-network acceptance.

evidence-and-limits.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/evidence-and-limits-01
evidence-and-limits.text: The checks that run on every pull request cover different claims. The off-chain lint app formats every command module and runs HLint over all of them, journey and update-terminal included, with no directory exclusions (see Checking off-chain code). The component build compiles all four commands. The registry workflow runs the journey from the checkout with a freshly built blueprint, and runs each archive command from an extracted release archive with its jq assertion over the observation. The supported deployment identity check runs genesis-skey, deploy and verify on a local devnet, refuses a manifest whose representative policy was changed, and now also checks the verb router's refusals without a node, that --out=FILE writes the same key as --out FILE, and that count finds one registry output and exactly the reference outputs the manifest records.

evidence-and-limits.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/evidence-and-limits-02
evidence-and-limits.text: Named limits: the journey is exercised from the checkout only — running it from an extracted archive is issue #214 and is not shown here. No earlier observation of a successful count exists to compare against; its first executed evidence is this change's. The commands' narration, flags and JSON are command contracts that command runs establish; the registry transitions they submit are governed by the accepted Lean model through the library builders, and a green command run is not a proof of any model theorem. A build or a fixture does not establish an archive or live-chain claim.

the-deployment-verbs.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/the-deployment-verbs-01
the-deployment-verbs.text: Main keeps the outer handler and the router. Every verb reads its flags through Deployment.Options, which accepts --name value and --name=value alike and refuses each verb's missing required flag by name. The release's compiled halves and the one pin derivation are Deployment.Compiled; node operations are Deployment.Node; each verb is its own module under offchain/deployment/Deployment/. The usage text still names deploy and verify only, as it always did; the router accepts all four verbs. The manifest itself stays with the library facade described in Deployment record ownership.

the-journey-step-by-step.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/the-journey-step-by-step-01
the-journey-step-by-step.text: Booking and folding stay two narrated steps. This division introduces no narration hook and does not move the journey onto the driver; that decision belongs to issue #202 and remains open.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/the-story-this-serves-01
the-story-this-serves.text: As an operator, I run the registry journey from a checkout, the two archive commands insert-active and update-terminal from an extracted release archive, and deployment against a node. I need the same options, the same narration in the same order, the same observation JSON, the same refusals and the same exit status after their entry files are divided into owners, so the CI steps and release pages that read those outputs keep meaning what they meant.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/the-story-this-serves-02
the-story-this-serves.text: As a contributor, I want one visible owner for each option, scenario step and deliberate control, so I can change a command without searching a thousand-line file or accidentally changing another command's evidence.

the-two-archive-commands.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/the-two-archive-commands-01
the-two-archive-commands.text: insert-active books and folds one insertActive at a wallet, reads exactly one active token there, folds a fresh key as the accepting control, then requires a second booking of the same key to be refused. The control runs first because a refused request is never consumed and would poison the fold after it. Its owners are InsertActive.Options, InsertActive.Steps, InsertActive.Controls, InsertActive.Observation and InsertActive.Scenario.

the-two-archive-commands.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/the-two-archive-commands-02
the-two-archive-commands.text: update-terminal boots two registries in one session before any fold. In the first it inserts the story's key, retires it — burning the witness from the wallet input that held it and committing a Terminal leaf — and then requires a key bound absent to be refused retirement, the story's retirement being that refusal's control. In the second it retires an active control key, then requires a key the trie never bound to be refused. Each refusal needs a registry of its own because a refused fold leaves its request pending. Its owners are UpdateTerminal.Registry (session, boots, bookings, mirrored and deliberately inadmissible folds, roots), UpdateTerminal.Steps, UpdateTerminal.Controls, UpdateTerminal.Observation, UpdateTerminal.Scenario and the matching Options and Narration.

the-two-archive-commands.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/the-two-archive-commands-03
the-two-archive-commands.text: Every value in both observation documents is passed in from what the steps and controls executed or read back; the observation modules type no expected value.

which-way-dependencies-run.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/which-way-dependencies-run-01
which-way-dependencies-run.text: Every command follows this shape; no module imports its command's Main, and no command imports another command's modules. Where two commands carry the same small helper — the genesis submission, the registry configuration for a seed, the wallet read — each keeps its own copy: a shared owner across executables would be a library change, which this division does not make. The library remains the owner of every transaction the commands build, and its generated interface is the off-chain API reference; the command modules are executables, documented here with source links rather than in that reference.

who-calls-each-command.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/who-calls-each-command-01
who-calls-each-command.text: The release check requires both archive commands' Main.hs paths in the on-chain archive, and the archive carries every tracked file under offchain/, so the new modules travel with the entry files they serve. The executable names and entry paths are unchanged.

who-owns-a-registry-command.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/who-owns-a-registry-command-01
who-owns-a-registry-command.text: These four standalone runners have been removed from the command layer. This page records their former structure; its commands and evidence below are historical. Use the application command journey for the retained implementation.

who-owns-a-registry-command.name: docs-offchain-command-entrypoints/who-owns-a-registry-command-02
who-owns-a-registry-command.text: A contributor changing what one of the registry commands does — a flag, a narrated step, a field of the observation JSON, a deliberate refusal — wants to open the one module that owns that concern and have the review ask one question. Before this division, each command was a single entry file of up to 1417 lines, and a change to the journey's negative cases was reviewed beside its identity manifest parser and its proof checks. Now each command's Main.hs holds only its outer failure handler, and named command-local modules own the options, the steps, the deliberate controls and the observation. This page says which module to open, which way the dependencies run, what may never change while the code moves, who calls each command, and what the evidence does and does not show.

evidence-and-limits.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/evidence-and-limits-01
evidence-and-limits.text: The focused cage suite executes the rows above over files and a provider stub serving finite UTxOs; the devnet identity step rides the branch ruleset's required Build Gate status context — a normal, non-continue-on-error step on the open, synchronize and reopen pull-request runs of that job, so a refusal or a setup failure fails Build Gate itself — and boots a real devnet, deploys a registry, verifies the intact manifest end to end, and observes the real refusal and its diagnostic when the recorded representative policy is changed. The row stays open until the pushed PR head's Build Gate run shows the step executed and passed. Limits are named rather than implied: the focused rows exercise the library attachment path over a fixture, not a public journey, and no mirror-root comparison is claimed there; the retained register, recovery and retirement journeys are excluded from the classified component build and are covered by source-level caller mapping here, not by compilation in that carrier; the devnet identity step establishes same-release agreement between the manifest's pins and the release in hand, not cross-release stability of the identity producers; and the focused suite has no row for the mirror's JSON parse refusal, a process-window-only mismatch, or the representative-policy pin through attach. The mirror-root comparison itself remains executable only in the retained journeys, whose three-runner check cannot complete today, so its status is a named limit rather than a green row.

one-owner-per-record.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/one-owner-per-record-01
one-owner-per-record.text: The deployment command is one of those callers: its command-local modules — flag reading in Deployment.Options, release loading in Deployment.Compiled, node operations in Deployment.Node and the deploy, verify and count verbs — import the facade's names and nothing behind it, as described in Who owns a registry command.

one-owner-per-record.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/one-owner-per-record-02
one-owner-per-record.text: The facade re-exports exactly the surface callers already import; the three owners are package-internal modules of the same library, so the generated API reference documents them for the contributor while a caller keeps compiling against the facade. The mirror reads its path, its hex rendering and its error helper from the manifest owner, so .mirror.json has one definition; attachment reads manifest values and the output-reference parse from the same owner, plus the focused identity and lookup adapters the builders use, so a recorded address and a built address are derived the same way.

the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry-00
the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry.text: The boundary the record cannot carry.

the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry-01
the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry.text: Writing to a registry means proving a key against the registry's current trie, and that proof needs the whole trie, not the root the chain reports. The deployment carries it as the mirror file beside the manifest, written by each run and read by the next — the record's one non-chain dependency. That file is a hazard, so it is checked rather than hoped away, and the check belongs to the caller that attaches, not to the attach operation itself: after attaching, the retained journey callers load the mirror and compare its root with the chain's root, so a mirror that drifted — a run that died mid-fold, a copy belonging to another deployment — fails by that comparison instead of building proofs against a trie the chain does not have. The extraction does not move that comparison; moving it without a behavior and evidence contract would change the boundary.

the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry-02
the-boundary-the-record-cannot-carry.text: Attachment and verification stay two operations, not one. Both resolve the release pins, the token, the recorded reference outputs and the state output; verification then reads the live state datum and refuses a mismatched active policy or process and retract windows before reporting its claims, while attachment returns the resolved outputs without those additional checks. A run that attaches is not thereby verified — the journey callers' mirror comparison and the deployment command's verification are separate acts.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/the-story-this-serves-01
the-story-this-serves.text: As a registry operator, I record one deployment and attach a later run to it; I want the same manifest bytes, the same mirror path and contents, the same node checks, refusal messages and transaction effects after the code is divided into owners, so the files I already carry between machines keep working and a wrong registry is still refused by name. A contributor refactoring the record's home owes me that.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/the-story-this-serves-02
the-story-this-serves.text: What the focused suite executes — finite fixture cases, named here with their counts and limits: the manifest's JSON keys, its pretty bytes and trailing newline, the strict read error that names the file, every --deployment spelling and the environment fallback, the txid#index round trip with four named refusals, the mirror's path beside the manifest, its hex maps, its replacement write and its absent-file empty map, and the attachment path itself — one row resolving two recorded reference outputs and the state output in the order the manifest records them, reading the provider's query record back, and refusal rows observing the real named diagnostics for a reference output whose live script hash differs from the pin, one that is no longer live, one that carries no script at all, an unreadable recorded address, a seed whose derived token contradicts the manifest, a release whose state validator hash differs, a registry address with no recorded token, and the two live-state refusals only verification makes — the active policy and the process and retract windows. The mutation evidence is equally finite: before the move, six single-site source mutations on the unsplit module failed these counts — a hash-acceptance bypass one row, a reference reorder two rows, the mirror path one row, the manifest newline one row, a process-window- only check one row, the mirror newline one row; after the move, a field swap between the manifest's two address spellings failed eight of two hundred fifty rows, and a hash-acceptance bypass failed the one named refusal. Three branches have no focused row: the mirror's JSON parse refusal, a process-window-only window mismatch, and the representative-policy pin through attach itself — the devnet identity step executes that pin through verify, not attach. The out-of-range output index has no refusal row either: this toolchain's fixed-width read accepts out-of-range and negative indices, so the suite pins the four refusals the parse genuinely makes.

who-owns-a-deployment-record.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/who-owns-a-deployment-record-01
who-owns-a-deployment-record.text: The deployment mirror API remains for retained deployment journeys. Ordinary singular registry commands under #381 reconstruct proof state from public state-token history and do not read or write that mirror or a saved-root file. Demo 1 starts two independent users empty; joining by state token is delivered, with no shared directory. Importing a creator identity file is superseded.

who-owns-a-deployment-record.name: docs-offchain-deployment-owners/who-owns-a-deployment-record-02
who-owns-a-deployment-record.text: A contributor changing what a deployment carries — a manifest field, a mirror entry, the checks a run makes before it attaches to a recorded registry — wants to edit one module beside the concern it owns, and have the review ask one question. Before the extraction, all of it lived in one 677-line Deployment module where a JSON key change, a mirror persistence change and a node query change were reviewed side by side with nothing between them. Now the record has three focused owners behind the same public facade, and this page tells a contributor which owner their change belongs to, which way the dependencies run, what the record may never do while it moves, and where the evidence boundary sits.

checking-off-chain-code.name: docs-offchain-development/checking-off-chain-code-01
checking-off-chain-code.text: A contributor changing an off-chain component wants one repeatable way to find the source that CI checks and to see which supported components compile. A failed check should name the affected source or component. A passing check means only that its stated extent passed; the current maintenance work still has named lint and formatting gaps for the final epic integration.

current-boundaries.name: docs-offchain-development/current-boundaries-01
current-boundaries.text: The source inventory, formatter extent, HLint extent and component build extent are different claims. The nine retired naming runners have been removed with their Cabal declarations and flake exports: initialization, its refusals, maintenance, recovery, registration, retirement, repair and the two verification tools. Their old unverified inventory entries are removed as well; an absent component is not a successful build. The naming and registry libraries remain for their separate removal layer. Fourmolu and HLint continue to discover their complete remaining source extents without directory exclusions. The component carrier reports the components it actually builds, and runs no tests or commands. Historical receipts and the run pages in the old release archive describe their own revisions, not the current command surface.

module-ownership-maps.name: docs-offchain-development/module-ownership-maps-01
module-ownership-maps.text: The builder and blueprint modules, the runtime services, the registry fold and the four registry commands now each have a contributor map: which module owns a concern, where common edits land, and which decisions the extraction recorded. They are Builder and blueprint modules, Runtime service ownership, Who owns a registry fold and Who owns a registry command.

module-ownership-maps.name: docs-offchain-development/module-ownership-maps-02
module-ownership-maps.text: The final integration work for epic #272, tracked as #278, must remove these temporary gaps and put every tracked code source under actual lint and format checks. It must also cover repository code beyond off-chain Haskell. Until that work is accepted, use each command's stated extent when interpreting a green result. Any source correction still has to preserve the Lean model's behavior and the dependent consumer guarantees.

run-the-checks.name: docs-offchain-development/run-the-checks-01
run-the-checks.text: From the repository root, run the root build gate. Run the off-chain checks from offchain/ so Nix selects that flake:

run-the-checks.name: docs-offchain-development/run-the-checks-02
run-the-checks.text: The root build gate covers the root flake's model, site and other declared build checks. It does not build every off-chain Cabal component. The off-chain lint app runs Fourmolu and HLint on its stated source extents. The component build carrier compiles the library, its test components, and supported components used by current required workflows and shipped registry commands. It runs no executables or tests. Its inventory lists every Cabal declaration and explains which are built here, covered by another required job, or unbuildable or unverified. A failing included member makes the carrier fail; a green result does not mean that every Cabal component builds. The measured counts move with the tree — the provider retirement removed the node-internal declaration — so compare each claim with the carrier's next actual output rather than an earlier receipt.

where-the-source-list-comes-from.name: docs-offchain-development/where-the-source-list-comes-from-00
where-the-source-list-comes-from.text: Where the source list comes from.

where-the-source-list-comes-from.name: docs-offchain-development/where-the-source-list-comes-from-01
where-the-source-list-comes-from.text: offchain/nix/checks.nix reads every hs-source-dirs declaration in offchain/singular-registry.cabal at lint run time and adds the standalone signing controls. Every library, command and test component declares its source root. Discovery deduplicates nested directories and fails if it finds no sources or a declared directory is absent. Fourmolu uses the committed fourmolu.yaml, and HLint visits the same discovered files with no directory exclusions. Adding a component must update the Cabal declaration that makes it discoverable; the next lint run reports its actual extent. The format controls run from the repository root: a source accepted by formatter defaults but rejected by the house configuration must fail the check, its formatter correction must pass, and a tree without the configuration must fail loudly.

where-the-source-list-comes-from.name: docs-offchain-development/where-the-source-list-comes-from-02
where-the-source-list-comes-from.text: offchain/flake.nix derives a supported build set from the current workflow and currently supported command closure. Its inventory must account for every Cabal library, executable, and test suite, and the gate must fail when a new declaration has no classification or an omitted classification drifts. Its component manifest can be compared with the Cabal stanzas. The flake's command is the same command used by the off-chain component CI job.

choices-and-verification-limits.name: docs-offchain-fold-responsibilities/choices-and-verification-limits-01
choices-and-verification-limits.text: The state-fold and application request-fold suites exercise the current builders against compiled validators and altered-input controls. The packaged journey checks connected registration, update and termination on a private development chain. These are separate evidence boundaries; see the consumer record for requirements still uncovered.

choices-and-verification-limits.name: docs-offchain-fold-responsibilities/choices-and-verification-limits-02
choices-and-verification-limits.text: Browse the generated API reference for signatures and source, and the command guide for caller-visible receipts and selection behavior.

from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch.name: docs-offchain-fold-responsibilities/from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch-00
from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch.text: From a pending request to a batch.

from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch.name: docs-offchain-fold-responsibilities/from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch-01
from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch.text: The fold discovers pending requests through the application adapter and checks each against the selected registry and trie. Automatic selection skips individually unfoldable requests and keeps the first foldable request for each key. An explicitly selected batch is built in the requested order or refused; it is never silently trimmed.

from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch.name: docs-offchain-fold-responsibilities/from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch-02
from-a-pending-request-to-a-batch.text: The lineage owner reconstructs the registry trie from public history. The assembly owner constructs state continuation, request spends, token effects, committed holdings, rewards, validity and collateral. The application adapter supplies request recognition and spending rules. No booker's local file is an input to the fold.

who-owns-a-registry-fold.name: docs-offchain-fold-responsibilities/who-owns-a-registry-fold-01
who-owns-a-registry-fold.text: As a contributor changing a fold, you want the owner of each decision to be clear. The registry owns the state transition and batch transaction. The application owns recognition of a pending request, its spending script and its approval burn. The folder supplies public chain data and its own wallet.

how-pages-are-read.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/how-pages-are-read-01
how-pages-are-read.text: The listing calls are read page by page, each page asking for an exact row total, in a stable order: output reference for the output listings, block height then transaction id for the asset history.

how-pages-are-read.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/how-pages-are-read-02
how-pages-are-read.text: The client stops when the rows read reach the total, or at the first page shorter than the limit, and then requires the rows read to equal the total. Each of these refuses the whole call as an incomplete page, and never returns a shorter answer as a whole one: a body cut off or not one JSON document, a page with more rows than the limit, a range that does not name the rows at the offset asked for, an answer with no exact total, a total that changes between pages, fewer rows than the total, and more pages than the configured ceiling. The public preprod service answers an exact total on every listing call when asked for one.

recorded-answers-and-the-recorder.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/recorded-answers-and-the-recorder-01
recorded-answers-and-the-recorder.text: singular-koios probe runs read requests against a Koios URL and prints the decoded facts of each, or the named failure. singular-koios record runs the same requests and writes every raw answer they take, page by page, as one fixture file holding the request, the Koios schema revision, the time and the SHA-256 of the body. Its requests name read calls only; submission is not one of them, and the recording transport refuses one without sending it. The token file is read before anything is sent, the schema document included, and the schema document is fetched under the same timeout and retry bounds as every call. Request headers are not recorded; answer headers are, and the live transport replaces the token in header names, header values, bodies and exception text before returning an exchange. It recognises literal characters and JSON escapes, including mixed Unicode escapes and escaped slashes, even in an incomplete JSON body. Bytes outside each match are preserved. A server that echoes an accepted token back therefore cannot put that copy into a fixture, a failure or its printed log text. An answer the client refuses for its content — an absent fact, an answer that does not decode — is recorded all the same, and recording goes on: the tests judge it. A directory or file that cannot be written is a named refusal.

recorded-answers-and-the-recorder.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/recorded-answers-and-the-recorder-02
recorded-answers-and-the-recorder.text: The schema revision is the info.version of the koiosapi.yaml document Koios serves at the origin of the base URL. Loading a fixture directory refuses a fixture whose body does not match its hash, fixtures recorded under different schema revisions, two fixtures for one request, and an empty directory.

recorded-answers-and-the-recorder.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/recorded-answers-and-the-recorder-03
recorded-answers-and-the-recorder.text: The preprod set under offchain/test/fixtures/koios/preprod/ is recorded by just koios-fixtures from https://preprod.koios.rest/api/v1 with read calls only. The tests replay it through the recorded transport and through the HTTP transport pointed at a loopback server serving the same answers, and both must decode identically. A loopback server in the test suite also produces rate limiting, slow answers, cut-off and missing pages, server errors, refused tokens and refused submissions on demand, and the tests count the attempts it receives.

the-koios-client.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-koios-client-01
the-koios-client.text: A provider author building the Koios instance of the ledger provider wants one Koios client that the recorded answers in continuous integration and the live public service both go through, so that a test that passes on a recording says something about the live service. A user on a busy public endpoint wants every command to finish or to stop with a named reason, never to continue on half an answer presented as a whole one. This page shows how the client is put together, what each call returns, how pages are read, why a call stops, and what the recorded evidence does and does not establish.

the-modules.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-modules-01
the-modules.text: The client is three modules of the public off-chain library and one public sublibrary, koios-http, that holds everything touching the network. The main library gains no network dependency.

the-modules.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-modules-02
the-modules.text: Singular.Provider.Koios.Wire describes one request per Koios call and decodes each answer into Conway ledger types. It performs no request.

the-modules.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-modules-03
the-modules.text: Singular.Provider.Koios.Client defines the transport — one request in, one raw answer and its attempt count out — and builds every typed call on it: it pages, classifies the status and decodes, once, for every transport.

the-modules.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-modules-04
the-modules.text: Singular.Provider.Koios.Recorded answers from a fixture directory. A request with no fixture is named as not recorded.

the-modules.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-modules-05
the-modules.text: The HTTP transport, Singular.Provider.Koios.Http in the koios-http sublibrary (source), sends requests to a base URL with an optional bearer token, a timeout on every attempt and bounded retries.

the-modules.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-modules-06
the-modules.text: The recorder and probe, Singular.Provider.Koios.Recorder in the same sublibrary (source), run read requests named on the command line and either print their decoded facts or write every raw answer as a fixture.

the-modules.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-modules-07
the-modules.text: The two koios-http modules are documented here by their source, because the generated reference covers the main library only.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-story-this-serves-01
the-story-this-serves.text: As a provider author, I import a Koios client that knows nothing of registries or of the ledger-provider interface, and I choose its transport: recorded answers for the test suite, or the live HTTP service. Both hand the client the same raw answers — status, headers and body — so the same code pages and decodes both, and a fixture and a live answer cannot be read two different ways.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-story-this-serves-02
the-story-this-serves.text: As a user with a Koios account, I give the client my bearer token in a file. After surrounding white space is stripped, it must contain at least 32 ASCII characters: letters, digits and -._~+/, with optional = padding at the end, and at least one character outside 0123456789abcdefABCDEF. An all-hexadecimal token could occur in a fixture's SHA-256 metadata even after its echoed copies were removed, so it is refused too. A short or empty token, a substring of the redaction marker <token>, or a token containing other characters is refused as TokenFileInvalid before any request, including the recorder's schema request. The refusal explains the restriction without printing the token. For an accepted token, the client replaces echoed copies in returned answers, failures and recorded fixtures; the command line names only its file, and the failure text printed to logs carries no echoed credential.

the-story-this-serves.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/the-story-this-serves-03
the-story-this-serves.text: As a user on a busy endpoint, I see a call either answer or stop with one named reason: unreachable, timed out, rate limited, server failing, refused by the server, an incomplete page, an unknown fact, or an answer that does not decode at a named position. An address with no outputs is an empty answer, not a failure.

what-each-call-returns.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/what-each-call-returns-01
what-each-call-returns.text: Submission through submitTx takes the existing SignedTx type, whose hidden constructor is reached through signTx with a payment signing key. The client serializes that signed transaction as Conway CBOR, preserving its body and witnesses. It accepts no unsigned transaction or raw byte string through this call. The type establishes that a payment-key witness was added; the ledger still decides whether the transaction is valid.

what-each-call-returns.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/what-each-call-returns-02
what-each-call-returns.text: Koios reports a datum hash for an output that carries an inline datum too; the inline datum wins. A reference script must hash to the script hash Koios names. A transaction that failed its scripts is returned with its validity false, never dropped. The order of asset_txs makes pages stable; it is not the order in which the asset was passed on, because Koios gives no position within a block and a transaction that included an asset need not have spent it.

what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-it-does-not-00
what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.text: What the evidence establishes, and what it does not.

what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-it-does-not-01
what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.text: Each recorded output is compared with the output at the same index of its producing transaction, decoded by the ledger from that transaction's recorded bytes, and the set of output references is compared with the producer's — the raw recorded rows for a listing, the transaction's own inputs, reference inputs and outputs for tx_info — so a decoder that changes, drops or adds an output fails. The protocol parameters decoded from epoch_params must equal the ledger's own reading of the node-form parameters Koios serves for the same epoch.

what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-it-does-not-02
what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.text: The recorded set is one day's snapshot of public preprod and covers the shapes it holds: key and script addresses, ada-only and multi-asset values, inline datums, datum hashes and Plutus V3 reference scripts. Plutus V1 or V2 reference scripts, Byron addresses and pointer addresses are not in it. Koios gives no bytes for a native (timelock) reference script, only a summary of it, so an output holding one cannot be decoded exactly: the client refuses it by name, as the recorded preprod answer in the set shows. A caller that reads such outputs cannot use this client for them. No transaction that failed its scripts was found on preprod, so a recorded transaction with its validity flag cleared stands in for one; its id hashes the body alone and is unchanged. The live preprod service does not send the valid_contract field its published schema lists for tx_cbor and tx_info; validity comes from the transaction's own bytes and from the per-script flags Koios does send. A body cut off on the connection is retried and named in code, but the loopback server cannot produce one, so only the client's mapping of it is tested.

what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-it-does-not-03
what-the-evidence-establishes-and-what-i.text: The token checks generate accepted bearer credentials containing text from the redaction marker, header names and JSON literals, alongside arbitrary characters from the full accepted alphabet. Coverage checks require each adversarial family, padding, slashes and credentials that can also name HTTP headers to occur. A loopback server echoes each credential literally and through Unicode escapes; the checks inspect status, header names, header values, body bytes, failure and probe renderings, and the actual fixture files with their JSON encoding. Generated all-hexadecimal credentials are refused too. Refused credentials must produce zero server requests, both for the transport and for the recorder. The fixed credentials remain examples. These generated cases are local evidence over sampled inputs, not a formal proof over all credentials or evidence of public-service behavior.

why-a-call-stops.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/why-a-call-stops-01
why-a-call-stops.text: Every failure names the call, the attempts the transport made and the evidence. Retries live in the HTTP transport, so a recorded replay never sleeps. A submission is retried only when no answer arrived — unreachable or timed out — because resending the same signed bytes cannot apply them twice; a 400 at submission is the server's refusal of that transaction and is returned as its text after one attempt.

why-a-call-stops.name: docs-offchain-koios-client/why-a-call-stops-02
why-a-call-stops.text: The HTTP transport's bounds are configuration values. Their defaults are a 20 second timeout per attempt, five attempts, delays doubling from a quarter second up to eight seconds with jitter, a rate-limit wait honoured up to 30 seconds, and 60 seconds for a whole request, retries included. That ceiling bounds the elapsed time: no retry starts past it, and each attempt's timeout is cut to what remains of it.

one-owner-per-runtime-concern.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/one-owner-per-runtime-concern-01
one-owner-per-runtime-concern.text: The runtime's owners are three public components. local-services owns the generic session and the fixed services computed from it; the main library owns the registry's application services and the bounds a command runs under; and koios-http owns the one live terminal composition and its transport. The generic ledger capabilities — the session, its evidence, and the services computed from raw facts — know nothing of a registry's application, and no shipped module names a node.

one-owner-per-runtime-concern.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/one-owner-per-runtime-concern-02
one-owner-per-runtime-concern.text: The first twelve rows live in local-services, the next three in the main library, the following three in koios-http, and the last in the command line. The trie's own owners — TrieState and its instances — are a separate capability documented with the library's modules in the off-chain API reference; the main library's re-exports of Ledger, LedgerProvider, Evidence and Signing keep their stable import paths, and their generated pages come from local-services' own Haddock tree.

runtime-service-ownership.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/runtime-service-ownership-01
runtime-service-ownership.text: A contributor changing how the registry's off-chain commands obtain their ledger facts — a different wallet, a longer confirmation window, a new provider transport, a change to what a command reports about its reads — wants one obvious owner per concern, so the change is reviewed in one place and a fact or a wait can never quietly exist twice. This page maps the provider-era runtime to its owners: what each module is responsible for, where common changes land, and what the checks establish about the split.

runtime-service-ownership.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/runtime-service-ownership-02
runtime-service-ownership.text: The node runtime this page once mapped is retired. The package-private node-internal library — its read adapter, in-memory chain, session runner and indexer — no longer exists, and with it the public Singular.Registry.Node facade: no shipped command opens a node, holds a socket or keeps a chain index. That retirement is the provider migration's own record, with its operator rulings, in the provider ticket's decisions; this page describes what replaced it.

what-the-checks-establish.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/what-the-checks-establish-01
what-the-checks-establish.text: A source check confines every backend name: a module outside the confinement allow list that names a node backend fails the build, and each allow-list entry carries its reason. The commands never hold that list. Submission is signed bytes only, every wait runs under the common bound, and the development network's own machinery — the private Koios-shaped facade, its raw-facts recorder and the generated devnet — is test infrastructure that never ships with the terminal.

what-the-checks-establish.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/what-the-checks-establish-02
what-the-checks-establish.text: What is deliberately not claimed here: the live Koios HTTP transport's production behaviour — its retries, rate limits and public URLs — is outside the provider ticket's scope and belongs to the Koios client ticket, #389, whose implementation main already carries in Provider.Koios.Http and Provider.Koios.Client. This page records who owns what; it accepts and verifies nothing of that transport's production behaviour.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-01
where-common-changes-land.text: A provider transport, its HTTP behaviour or the terminal composition: koios-http — Terminal, Provider.Koios.Http — with ProviderSettings parsing what the operator supplies.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-02
where-common-changes-land.text: A read, its evidence or its verdict: LedgerProvider, Evidence or SessionEvidence in local-services. The witness type stays a parameter; Demo 1 ships the uninhabited one and the unverified verifier.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-03
where-common-changes-land.text: Local evaluation or time conversion: SessionServices, LocalEvaluation, NetworkTime or TimeMaterial. An adapter supplies facts and cannot select an evaluator or a time converter.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-04
where-common-changes-land.text: A bounded wait, its failure or the submission bound: Wait, whose failure identity WaitTypes fixes. The common submission and confirmation bounds live here; a transport's per-request bound remains its adapter's concern, never an await of the chain.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-05
where-common-changes-land.text: Confirmation of a submitted transaction: Confirmation, under the common bounded polling — never a provider-owned await.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-06
where-common-changes-land.text: The pre-run funding floor or its diagnostic: Funding.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-07
where-common-changes-land.text: Wallet loading, key handling or signing: Wallet and Signing. Key bytes are never logged.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-08
where-common-changes-land.text: What the provider boundary reports: typed events into the tracer the caller hands it — ProviderTrace, Trace and TraceRender.

where-common-changes-land.name: docs-offchain-node-ownership/where-common-changes-land-09
where-common-changes-land.text: How a command reaches its capabilities, or what its journal records: Singular.CLI.Session beside the terminal composition.

current-command-records.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/current-command-records-01
current-command-records.text: Creation and folds use the state records. Registration, updates, termination booking and registration exits use the application records. Their owning builders construct datums and redeemers, then evaluate transactions against the corresponding compiled validators.

current-command-records.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/current-command-records-02
current-command-records.text: Changing a representation starts with its behavioral authority and the contract that consumes it. Constructor indices, field order and nesting are part of the wire. A Haskell codec change alone cannot establish agreement with a validator. Literal codec tests, compiled-validator tests and connected journeys check different boundaries.

evidence-and-navigation.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/evidence-and-navigation-01
evidence-and-navigation.text: The Types suite checks literal encodings and decodings. The state and application builder suites separately exercise their compiled validators. Connected journeys check transactions at the ledger boundary. The consumer record publishes the requirements still uncovered; a codec test does not close those rows.

evidence-and-navigation.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/evidence-and-navigation-02
evidence-and-navigation.text: Use the API reference to find the signatures and source for each owner. The builder guide maps construction paths, and the fold guide describes the boundary between registry state and application request rules.

shared-values-and-retained-adapters.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/shared-values-and-retained-adapters-01
shared-values-and-retained-adapters.text: Singular.Registry.Types remains a facade for shared proof steps, edge ordinals, output references and generic adapter codecs. Public-history readers, recovery adapters and synthetic library tests still use these representations. Decoding a historical record does not establish support for its former validator or command.

shared-values-and-retained-adapters.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/shared-values-and-retained-adapters-02
shared-values-and-retained-adapters.text: The shared family has separate owners for primitive values, proofs and records. This diagram groups those responsibilities; the generated reference provides the exact module imports and signatures.

shared-values-and-retained-adapters.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/shared-values-and-retained-adapters-03
shared-values-and-retained-adapters.text: These generic codecs are separate from the current state and application record owners above. The shared proof and edge vocabulary also remains in use by the current trie capability. Removing obsolete transaction builders does not remove these retained callers.

who-owns-the-registry-wire.name: docs-offchain-wire-types/who-owns-the-registry-wire-01
who-owns-the-registry-wire.text: As a contributor changing a wire representation, you want to find the codec used by the command you are changing. The current registry state is encoded by Singular.State.Records. The current application's requests and live holdings are encoded by OpenDatum.Requests.Records.

coverage-limits.name: docs-onchain-api-reference/coverage-limits-01
coverage-limits.text: A module has a generated page when it declares a public definition. Test cases and a validator with no public declarations remain available in the source tree. The application's separate on-chain project has no generated reference on this site; that coverage gap remains explicit. Compilation and generated documentation do not establish validator behavior or ledger acceptance.

follow-a-rule.name: docs-onchain-api-reference/follow-a-rule-01
follow-a-rule.text: The state validator owners page maps creation, request handling, state recognition and token naming to their source owners. Test support appears in the reference because its helpers are public to test modules; it is not an additional product interface.

follow-a-rule.name: docs-onchain-api-reference/follow-a-rule-02
follow-a-rule.text: The documentation build generates the interface and binds its pages to source digests. Its checks reject a missing page, changed source or a source link to another revision.

open-a-module.name: docs-onchain-api-reference/open-a-module-01
open-a-module.text: The reference's index lists every documented module and searches its public members. These links open the generated pages on the site and the source files when read in the repository.

validator-api-reference.name: docs-onchain-api-reference/validator-api-reference-01
validator-api-reference.text: A contributor can open each registry module's generated interface, follow its public declarations and inspect their source at the documentation build's exact revision. The reference is generated by the pinned Aiken compiler from the same source tree as this page.

check-a-change.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/check-a-change-01
check-a-change.text: Run the registry Aiken tests and identity check from onchain/. The application tests run in a composed assembly so they can call both validators. The root script-hash-comparison command checks both separate builds, their identity manifests and the merged deployment blueprint, with controls that must refuse moved hashes and differing merged script bytes.

check-a-change.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/check-a-change-02
check-a-change.text: Compilation and Aiken tests do not establish a connected ledger lifecycle or full model correspondence. The development-network journeys and the published conformance record state their separate evidence and gaps.

registry-owners.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/registry-owners-01
registry-owners.text: The validator dispatches creation and request handling to their owners. Shared state recognition and token names are defined once in the registry library.

who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/who-owns-a-state-validator-rule-00
who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.text: Who owns a state validator rule.

who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.name: docs-onchain-validator-owners/who-owns-a-state-validator-rule-01
who-owns-a-state-validator-rule.text: A contributor changing a registry rule can find its source owner and the checks that exercise it here. The registry validator and the application request validator are compiled independently, then combined into the deployment blueprint.

choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.name: docs-payload-json/choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting-00
choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.text: Choose the form with the schema setting.

choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.name: docs-payload-json/choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting-01
choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.text: The setting has two values, plain and detailed, and plain when it is absent. It is not a standing setting: there is no environment variable and no key in the configuration file, because the form is a property of the file you give.

choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.name: docs-payload-json/choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting-02
choose-the-form-with-the-schema-setting.text: The refusal of a detailed file covers the whole document only. A detailed-looking object nested inside a larger document is plain JSON like any other: the file {"wrapper": {"int": 5}} is stored as a map from the text wrapper to a map from the text int to the integer 5. Every file the previous release accepted is therefore either refused with the instruction or read exactly as before when the setting is detailed; none is stored as a different datum.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-01
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: Reading a file in the plain schema turns its JSON into Plutus data by these rules, and by nothing else, so you can apply them by hand.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-02
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: A whole number becomes the integer. A number written 1.0 or 5e2 is a whole number too and is stored as 1 and 500; the way the number was written is not kept. A number may have at most a thousand digits.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-03
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: A text becomes the byte string of its UTF-8. The empty text is the empty byte string.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-04
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: true becomes the constructor with index 1 and no fields, which is the Plutus boolean, and false becomes the constructor with index 0 and no fields.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-05
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: An array becomes the list of its items, mapped in order. The empty array is the empty list.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-06
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: An object becomes the map from each key, as a byte string of its UTF-8, to its value, mapped. The entries are in ascending order of the key bytes, whatever order the file wrote them in. The empty object is the empty map.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-07
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: null and a number with a fraction are refused.

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-08
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: A whole file is accepted, not only an object: the file may hold 42, "alice" or [1, 2].

how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.name: docs-payload-json/how-ordinary-json-becomes-data-09
how-ordinary-json-becomes-data.text: Worked by hand, the file {"answer": 42} holds one object with one key, so the data is a map with one entry. The key is the byte string of the text answer, whose bytes are 616e73776572 in hex, and the value is the integer 42. In the detailed schema that is {"map":[{"k":{"bytes":"616e73776572"},"v":{"int":42}}]}. The file 42 is the integer 42, the same data as the detailed {"int":42}.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-01
limits.text: null is not stored. A later release may accept it without changing what is stored today.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-02
limits.text: The text of a number is not kept: 1.0 is read back as 1.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-03
limits.text: An object's key order in the file is not kept; the stored order is ascending by key bytes, because JSON readers do not preserve it and a map in Plutus data is ordered. A key repeated in the file keeps its first value, as the JSON reader does.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-04
limits.text: A payload with a byte string that is not text, a map with keys that are not text or any constructor other than the two booleans needs the detailed schema, and it prints in the detailed schema.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-05
limits.text: A text stored as bytes by the detailed schema reads back as text when the bytes are valid UTF-8; nobody can tell from the chain which form wrote it.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-06
limits.text: A whole payload that looks like a detailed document, such as {"int": 5} as a plain object, cannot be written in the plain schema because of the refusal above. It can be stored through the detailed schema as a map with the text key, and it then reads back as plain JSON; writing that JSON again needs the detailed form.

limits.name: docs-payload-json/limits-07
limits.text: The settings table in connecting singular to a ledger provider lists --payload and --payload-schema with the commands that take them.

store-a-document.name: docs-payload-json/store-a-document-01
store-a-document.text: Write the file and give it to insert, with no schema setting:

store-a-document.name: docs-payload-json/store-a-document-02
store-a-document.text: Supply the registry, blueprint and provider settings as described in the registry command guide. Fold the pending reference the booking prints with open-datum fold --pending TXID#IX. update takes the same payload file and schema setting. Reading a key has replacement: none, issue 744.

store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.name: docs-payload-json/store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload-00
store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.text: Store ordinary JSON as a key's payload.

store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.name: docs-payload-json/store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload-01
store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.text: As a controller with a registry and a key, you store the document {"answer": 42} under the key by writing that file and nothing else. The holding carries the payload on chain. A reader has replacement: none, issue 744. You did not have to learn first how Plutus data is written in JSON. As an integrator who needs exact control of the bytes on chain, you keep writing the detailed schema, {"constructor": 0, "fields": [{"int": 42}]}, and say so on the command, so nothing is guessed. As someone with a script from the previous release, you find that your payload file in the detailed schema is refused with a sentence that tells you to say so, and is never stored as something else.

store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.name: docs-payload-json/store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload-02
store-ordinary-json-as-a-keys-payload.text: The first diagram shows how a file is read. The setting --payload-schema decides how the file becomes Plutus data: by the plain mapping of this page when the setting is plain or absent, and by the detailed schema, as before, when it is detailed. Either way the result is the same kind of value, Plutus data in the key's output on chain.

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-01
what-inspect-prints.text: open-datum inspect prints a live key's payload under payload in the application output, with the field payloadSchema beside it, and the update receipt prints the two fields the same way. A payload has a plain reading when it is one that the rules above could have produced:

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-02
what-inspect-prints.text: an integer of at most a thousand digits;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-03
what-inspect-prints.text: a byte string that is valid UTF-8, read as a text;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-04
what-inspect-prints.text: a list whose items all have a plain reading;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-05
what-inspect-prints.text: a map whose keys are valid UTF-8 byte strings in strictly ascending order of bytes and whose values all have a plain reading;

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-06
what-inspect-prints.text: the constructor with index 0 or 1 and no fields, read as false or true.

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-07
what-inspect-prints.text: When the stored data has a plain reading, payload is that JSON and payloadSchema is plain. Otherwise payload is the detailed schema of the data and payloadSchema is detailed: a byte string that is not text, a map with a key that is not text or with its keys out of order, any other constructor, or a number past the limit of a thousand digits.

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-08
what-inspect-prints.text: The reading is a property of the data, not of how it was stored. The detailed {"int":42} and the plain 42 store the same data, so both read back as 42. The current live envelope, with its protected control and payload in the detailed schema, is printed under envelope and datum, so the exact data is retained. The decoded control names its registry, key, controller, active asset and protected deposit; deposit also prints that amount in lovelace. Pending termination has no payload. Terminal and never registered describe the authenticated leaf; unavailable reads and refusals print their reasons.

what-inspect-prints.name: docs-payload-json/what-inspect-prints-09
what-inspect-prints.text: singular registry inspect reports neutral active custody and prints the datum as data under datum, with its inline, hash or none form under datumKind. It does not decode a payload. Both commands default to human text; use --json for these fields and --query-work for measured provider work. See reading a key for output and exit statuses.

what-is-refused.name: docs-payload-json/what-is-refused-01
what-is-refused.text: A refusal names the file, says what it asked for, and names the value and where it is, written as a path from the document: $ is the whole document, .name an object key and [2] an item. Every refusal comes before the node is read, so a preview with an unreachable node shows them too, and nothing is submitted.

coverage-boundary.name: docs-prior-art/coverage-boundary-01
coverage-boundary.text: These candidates warrant component-level evaluation once a reuse target is concrete. License compatibility, toolchain fit and correctness require their own checks; this comparison grants none of them. Reading a validator establishes what its source says, not what a deployment does. Singular remains a design with unimplemented conformance obligations. Continue with the naming walkthrough (historical) or protocol specification.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-01
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: AdaDomains. The whitepaper, sections 3–4 describes separate registry/domain state, pooled requests and address changes. Section 3.1 puts the list of minted domains in the datum of a one-shot registry token; section 3.3 records the two limits that follow — one minting transaction per registry per block, and roughly 1600 short domains before the 16kB transaction limit binds; section 4.1 answers them by hashing names and splitting registries dynamically, and section 4.2 by a pooling layer in which the user who triggers minting must mint every pooled request belonging to that registry. Project resolution documentation describes reading the domain datum. The inspected resolver SDK at 302235c supplies resolution code. These establish architectural precedent and a public resolver, not an inspected generic registry implementation. A root-hash map moves that size limit off the key set, but it does not decide Singular's batch policy, which remains an open decision. Historical throughput assertions are not adopted here.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-02
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: ADA Handle DeMi. At 1b5623c, mint/burn validation traverses MPF proofs and checks an allowed minter. The check is symmetric: can_mint_demi_handles requires the selected allowed_minter among the signatories, and can_burn_demi_handles requires any settings minter, so deletion from the root is gated exactly as issuance is. Order validation supplies execution, cancellation and refund conditions, including a distinct-output binding that prevents one owner output from satisfying several refunds. Mechanical overlap is useful; replacing application and governor rules is substantive work.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-03
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: Distributed Set. The validator at 4b0547a and utilities authenticate set changes with current mint/withdrawal invocation. The set is a linked list of sorted-value nodes, each holding its own node NFT, rather than a hashed map: its state lives in as many UTxOs as it has nodes, and a node is split when it grows. Its plain spend branch checks sortedness, the head and tail anchors, the node NFT and the unchanged datum fields, and carries a TODO where a check that existing values survive would go — so membership preservation rests entirely on the configured mint or stake script, not on the set validator. The sources also target the pre-cardano/transaction Aiken standard library, which reuse would have to migrate. They do not supply Singular's prior-action receipt and NFT custody lifecycle.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-04
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: CIP113. At 1e83ed9, the registry, issuance policy and programmable base provide relevant authentication and policy-binding techniques: a key must be the policy ID derived from the issuance template parameterised with its minting logic, registration requires that logic's withdraw-0, and custody is dispatched through a credential read live from the protocol-params datum. The registry's redeemers are RegistryInit and RegistryInsert, and its spend handler admits a node NFT mint only with a positive amount, otherwise requiring a continuing output — a registered key is never removed. Their live delegation and custody contract would require substantive adaptation.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-05
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: Masumi. The registry-v2 mint policy at ce96026 addresses generated asset identities and versioning: an asset name is a nonce byte, the hash of a consumed output reference and a three-byte version, an update burns a token and mints its successor at version plus one, and a burn needs only possession. That is a different uniqueness problem from a registry of application-selected keys; no shared state records which keys are taken.

evidence-and-useful-boundaries.name: docs-prior-art/evidence-and-useful-boundaries-06
evidence-and-useful-boundaries.text: CIP89's beacon pattern is also relevant precedent for minting that certifies an application UTxO: a beacon is minted only into a valid application output, burned when that output is spent, and never circulates. Singular's representative is the opposite in one respect that matters — it is held, moved between an application's own successive outputs, and carried into a terminal request — so the beacon rule cannot be adopted as stated, only its minting-time certification. A complete uniqueness, request and retirement protocol remains additional work.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-01
mpfs.text: MPFS is the nearest system to Singular and the one whose reuse must be answered explicitly, because Singular's map layer is MPF and the protocol specification already records, among its open decisions on transaction shapes and libraries, that old MPFS proofs are not proof of Singular's protocol. It is also the one candidate built as a component rather than as somebody's application: a cage is created by whoever consumes the seed, carries no application-specific rule, and serves whatever that creator puts in it. That posture is the one Singular copies. The difference is a single design decision inside it.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-02
mpfs.text: The inspected on-chain revision is cardano-mpfs-onchain at 34a5bfb. A cage is one NFT locked at the script address whose datum carries the MPF root. state.ak mints the cage token from a consumed seed, folds pending requests into a new root under Modify, and burns the cage under End. request.ak governs request UTxOs with Contribute, Retract and Sweep. shared.ak holds the authorization and phase predicates, and types.ak defines the request record and the map operations.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-03
mpfs.text: Four facts from that source decide the comparison.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-04
mpfs.text: Every spend of the state UTxO runs validateOwnership before the redeemer is examined, and that function requires the datum's single owner verification key hash among the transaction's signatories. Both Modify and End sit behind it.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-05
mpfs.text: Map entries are Operation values over ByteArray: Insert(value), Delete(value), Update(old, new). The cage mints exactly one token — its own state NFT — and no token is minted, burned or moved per key.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-06
mpfs.text: A request carries requestToken, requestOwner, the key, the operation, a tip and submitted_at. It commits to no application policy, no output shape and no approval; the only requester-side authorization anywhere in the validators is the Retract signature.

mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/mpfs-07
mpfs.text: Requests are governed by time. Contribute requires Phase 1 or rejectability, Retract requires the requester's signature inside Phase 2, and Sweep lets the owner clear any request that is not processable against the current state.

prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.name: docs-prior-art/prior-art-and-reuse-candidates-01
prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.text: Comparison date: 2026-09-09. Implementation links pin revisions; website and whitepaper references record the material inspected on that date. Every source cited below was fetched at its pinned revision and read against the claim it supports.

prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.name: docs-prior-art/prior-art-and-reuse-candidates-02
prior-art-and-reuse-candidates.text: The inspected projects provide substantial precedent for Singular's architecture and mechanics. No ready-made implementation of its complete contract was established in this bounded comparison. This is not a novelty claim, security audit or exhaustive search. Source inspection does not establish deployed behavior.

retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.name: docs-prior-art/retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key-00
retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.text: Retirement and reuse of a key.

retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.name: docs-prior-art/retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key-01
retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.text: Singular needs two ways for a registration to end, and the distinction is what makes the lifecycle worth managing centrally. Delete burns the representative and returns the key to absence, so a later approved Insert may register it again. Update burns the representative and writes Over, which is terminal: the key is retired permanently and no later Insert can revive it. Permanent retirement is the requirement that came from Singular's first consumer, where an identity must be able to end without its name being reissued to someone else.

retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.name: docs-prior-art/retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key-02
retirement-and-reuse-of-a-key.text: That requirement is not local to this project. CIP113 arrives at the same permanence from the other direction: its registry nodes are inserted and updated but never removed, so every registration it accepts is permanent whether or not permanence was wanted. Distributed Set leaves removal to the configured hook and specifies neither mode. MPFS supplies Delete, which frees the key, and nothing that retires one. No inspected system offers both modes under one contract, chosen per transition by the application that owns the entry.

the-authenticated-map-layer.name: docs-prior-art/the-authenticated-map-layer-01
the-authenticated-map-layer.text: This layer is the one part of Singular with ready implementations. The Aiken merkle-patricia-forestry library supplies on-chain proof verification, and is what both DeMi and MPFS build on; haskell-mts supplies the matching off-chain trie, proof generation and persistent storage. Choosing among these, or a different authenticated-set representation, does not resolve any of the open decisions, which are about certification, custody and retirement, not about how membership is proved.

what-remains-reusable-from-mpfs.name: docs-prior-art/what-remains-reusable-from-mpfs-01
what-remains-reusable-from-mpfs.text: The map layer and its off-chain machinery transfer; the authorization model does not. The fold shape — one proof per request applied against successive roots — is the shape Singular's permissionless fold requires. Off-chain, cardano-mpfs-offchain at 0f82465 supplies a cage indexer, a proof-bearing REST API, client transaction builders and cross-target verifiers over the same trie. Component-level reuse still needs its own evaluation: none of it was written against Singular's request or custody rules, and the decision on transaction shapes and shared libraries remains open.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-00
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: What Singular is trying to be.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-01
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: Singular is a component, not an application. A third party supplies one parameter — its application policy ID — and receives its own registry of unique keys with the representative NFT lifecycle managed end to end: minted into a certified application output on Insert, burned on retirement, burned and the key made available again on Delete. Nothing about the keys, the application's state or its business rules belongs to Singular.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-02
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: That is the axis on which the prior art has to be read, and most of it fails before authorization is reached. A registry welded to one application is not reusable by anyone else at any price short of forking and rewriting it; the code inspected below is mostly of that kind, however good it is at its own job. MPFS is the exception and the model: it is application-agnostic, anyone may create a cage, and its single blocking difference from Singular is that every cage has an owner.

what-singular-is-trying-to-be.name: docs-prior-art/what-singular-is-trying-to-be-03
what-singular-is-trying-to-be.text: Two further layers are worth keeping apart. The authenticated-map layer — a key set whose whole state fits in one datum and whose changes are proved on-chain — has working implementations that Singular can adopt; an equivalent registry would not be disqualified merely because it uses a different authenticated-set representation. The registry contract layer — who may change the map, what an entry certifies about an application output, and what token custody is coupled to a transition — is where every inspected system diverges.

why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.name: docs-prior-art/why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged-00
why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.text: Why Singular cannot adopt MPFS unchanged.

why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.name: docs-prior-art/why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged-01
why-singular-cannot-adopt-mpfs-unchanged.text: The phase design is worth separating from the verdict. MPFS uses time windows to keep the oracle's fold and the requester's retraction from racing, which is a real solution to a problem Singular shares. It is unavailable here for the same reason the rest is: the windows are exclusive to a named oracle, and Singular has none. In its place, Singular resolves races inside the fold — an Insert is checked against absence in the applicable successive registry state, and admission of a request asserts nothing about the key.

book-a-registration.name: docs-registry-commands/book-a-registration-01
book-a-registration.text: As Alice, you book a key with its payload and a deposit under a registry you name by its address, and the registry's configuration decides the deadlines.

book-a-registration.name: docs-registry-commands/book-a-registration-02
book-a-registration.text: The booking puts a pending registration at the request address of open datum. It holds the deposit (2 000 000 lovelace unless --deposit says more; a deposit below the minimum ADA of the output that will hold the key's token with its payload is refused, naming that minimum), the tip for whoever folds it (--tip, nothing by default), and its approval, the token that a fold, a reclaim or a cleanup consumes. The payload is the file --payload names, read in the form --payload-schema gives, plain JSON unless you say otherwise; store ordinary JSON as a key's payload gives the rules. --refund-address says where a reclaim or a cleanup returns the value, and it is your own address when you do not say.

book-a-registration.name: docs-registry-commands/book-a-registration-03
book-a-registration.text: The receipt names the pending registration, its approval, the key, the deposit, the tip, the refund address and the three times that matter: when it was booked, its processing deadline, and the end of its reclaim window. Whoever folds it, or you taking it back, can name the pending registration with --pending. A folder can also discover it from public approvals.

book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.name: docs-registry-commands/book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it-00
book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.text: Book permanent termination, then fold it.

book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.name: docs-registry-commands/book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it-01
book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.text: As Alice, you choose your live holding and book permanent termination. Its protected deposit is donated to the treasury in this transaction. The new request has no datum and holds exactly the active token and one termination approval; its ADA is the reward available to the folder. The active token moves into this request and is not burned at booking. There is no reclaim or cancellation window for this booking.

book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.name: docs-registry-commands/book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it-02
book-permanent-termination-then-fold-it.text: The receipt names the pending output and the treasuryDonation in lovelace. As Bob, you fold that pending output with open-datum fold, using --pending TXID#IX and your own vault. You need the public chain and your wallet; Alice's key, local directory and records are unnecessary.
