The fold burns the active token and the approval, creates no replacement holding, and leaves the key terminal permanently. You receive the request's whole value; your ordinary wallet input pays the transaction fee. A batch may mix terminations with registrations of other keys. A termination has no processing deadline.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-01
create-a-registry.text: As Carol, you spend one output of your wallet to make a registry, and the output you spend fixes the registry's identity.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-02
create-a-registry.text: The creation diagram shows what the command does. The command reads your wallet and looks for live reference copies of the validators. The first registry of an application publishes each in its own transaction, state first, and waits for both before it creates the registry. If you stop between publications, a rerun finds the live copy and publishes only the missing script. A later registry finds both live copies and sends one transaction. The registry's state token appears on the first output of the creation, and the command reads it back before it prints the receipt.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-03
create-a-registry.text: open-datum create makes a registry of open datum. Five parameters are fixed here for the life of the registry: the processing time and the reclaim time of a booked registration (--process-time and --reclaim-time), the widest validity interval a booking may declare (--booking-width), and the registration cost and the minimum tip (--registration-cost and --minimum-tip), which the registry carries and nothing enforces.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-04
create-a-registry.text: singular registry create makes the registry of any application whose policy you give with --application-policy: the policy is the one parameter of the state validator. The command publishes the state validator when no live copy of it exists, and creates the registry whose state token that validator guards.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-05
create-a-registry.text: The seed is your wallet's largest ada-only output, chosen when the registry is built and after the validators have been published when they had to be, so the publication cannot have spent it. --seed names another output of your wallet. The wallet funds the transactions and keeps their change. The builders choose the funding, so these commands refuse --fund-input, --max-outlay and --preview by name rather than ignore them.

create-a-registry.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-06
create-a-registry.text: The receipt names the registry's address and fingerprint, its state token, the seed, the output that now holds the state, the registry's root, the policy of the application, each validator with the output that carries its reference script and whether this command published it, and every transaction the command sent with what became of it.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-00
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: Create a registry and manage its keys on the proved design.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-01
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: As Carol, you create a registry for an application with one command and read its address and its state token from the receipt. As Alice, you book the registration of a key with its payload and a deposit, and the receipt names the pending registration the booking made. As Bob, you fold the registrations you name into the registry from the chain alone, and keep what each of them holds above its deposit. As Alice again, when nobody folds your registration you take it back inside its reclaim window, and when that window has passed anyone can clean it up and your deposit goes back to the refund address you chose. When a command is interrupted, the next write of the same wallet settles what it left, and nothing is ever sent a second time.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-02
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: The first three diagrams show the exits of one registration. A booking makes it pending. Until its processing deadline only a fold can spend it. After the deadline, and until the reclaim window ends, only the refund address can take it back. After the window anyone can clean it up.

create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.name: docs-registry-commands/create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on-the-proved-design-03
create-a-registry-and-manage-its-keys-on.text: This page describes ten commands: singular registry create, open-datum create, open-datum fold, open-datum insert, open-datum reclaim and open-datum cleanup, open-datum update and open-datum terminate, singular registry inspect and open-datum inspect. Every flag they take is listed with its description and its default in the settings table, and each command prints the same information with --help.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-00
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: Fold registrations and terminations into the registry.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-01
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: As Bob, give the registry and your wallet to discover its pending registrations and terminations from public approvals. You need nothing from anyone who booked them. The command orders requests by your take, greatest first, breaking ties by output reference. It skips requests that cannot individually fold in the observed state, then builds the greatest fitting prefix of the foldable rest. Use --limit to cap the number of automatically selected requests.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-02
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: This is the path of a successful discovered batch. Holders the application does not accept are kept in the accounting as skipped, with their references and reasons. A recognized request is also skipped when its key is already registered, its termination key is not active, its deposit is below the minimum the holding must keep, or its processing window has closed. The first individually foldable request for a key in take order keeps that key; later foldable requests for it are skipped as duplicates. An unfoldable earlier request never reserves the key. Every holder is folded, skipped with a reason, or left as a foldable request beyond the selected prefix.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-03
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: Transaction bytes include all required signing witnesses. Only transaction size, memory or steps exceeding the observed network limit permits trying a shorter prefix. A failed public read, registry replay or other transaction construction failure stops the fold with its own reason; it never becomes an empty or shorter discovered answer.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-04
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: Each registration burns its approval and receives its committed holding, active token and deposit. Its held value above that deposit is yours. A termination burns its approval and active token and pays its whole held value to you. Your wallet pays the transaction fee. Both kinds can share one batch with distinct keys.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-05
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: To choose the entire batch yourself, repeat --pending "$first" --pending "$second" instead. The command builds those requests in that order or refuses them, naming the reason; it never trims an explicit batch, even with --limit.

fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.name: docs-registry-commands/fold-registrations-and-terminations-into-the-registry-06
fold-registrations-and-terminations-into.text: The successful receipt names the registry's new root and state output. Its folded list gives each key, request kind and pending reference; skipped gives each unaccepted or individually unfoldable holder's reference and reason; left counts foldable requests not included. Skipped requests are never counted as left. If nothing can fold, the command refuses with nothing to fold and still names every skipped holder. A failed read remains unavailable and never claims an empty answer.

read-a-key.name: docs-registry-commands/read-a-key-01
read-a-key.text: As a reader, give the registry address and a key to either inspect command. No signer, blueprint or local state directory is needed.

read-a-key.name: docs-registry-commands/read-a-key-02
read-a-key.text: The neutral command identifies the application from the packaged release table and answers active, terminal or never registered, or reports an unavailable read or a refusal with its reason. Active custody includes its datum as data. The application command decodes a live holding's protected control, deposit and payload, or identifies pending termination. Both retain the authenticated state requirement for absence and every neutral refusal.

read-a-key.name: docs-registry-commands/read-a-key-03
read-a-key.text: Human text is the default; --json selects one JSON object. --query-work adds measured calls, rows and bytes per provider read and in total. Answers exit 0, unavailable reads exit 1, and refused evidence or invalid command lines exit 2. See reading a key for settings, classification order, refusal reasons and measurement limits.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-00
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: Take a registration back, or clean it up.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-01
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: As Alice, you take back a registration you booked while its reclaim window is open.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-02
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: Everything the registration holds returns to its refund address, which must be the wallet that runs the command, and its approval is burned. Before the window opens or after it closes the command is refused, saying when.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-03
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: As anyone, you clean up an expired registration once its reclaim window has ended.

take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.name: docs-registry-commands/take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up-04
take-a-registration-back-or-clean-it-up.text: The deposit returns to the refund address, the wallet that runs the command keeps what the request holds above the deposit, and the approval is burned. Both commands name exactly one pending registration.

update-a-live-holding.name: docs-registry-commands/update-a-live-holding-01
update-a-live-holding.text: As Alice, you choose the output that holds your active key and replace its payload. The control stays the same: its registry, active token, key, controller and protected deposit. The holding keeps all its tokens and at least the deposit. If the larger datum needs more minimum ADA, your wallet supplies it. No registry state is spent by the update.

update-a-live-holding.name: docs-registry-commands/update-a-live-holding-02
update-a-live-holding.text: The receipt names the new holding output. Use that reference for a later update or termination. A missing holding, another controller, or another named registry is refused before the transaction is signed.

when-a-command-is-interrupted.name: docs-registry-commands/when-a-command-is-interrupted-01
when-a-command-is-interrupted.text: As any of the three, you may lose the connection, stop the command, or run past --confirm-timeout. The command never sends a transaction twice.

when-a-command-is-interrupted.name: docs-registry-commands/when-a-command-is-interrupted-02
when-a-command-is-interrupted.text: The recovery diagram shows what happens to a transaction that was in flight. Every transaction is written to the journal under its identity before it is sent. If the command is interrupted, whatever the moment, the transaction keeps that identity. The next write of the same wallet for the same registry reads its journal before it builds anything. A transaction the chain holds is recorded as landed and named under reconciled in the next receipt, and a transaction the node refused stays recorded as refused. A transaction the chain does not yet show stops the next write, naming it, and nothing is built or sent until it is settled. A creation is journalled under the application and the wallet, because the name of the registry it makes is known only once its seed is chosen; the other commands are journalled under the registry.

when-a-command-is-interrupted.name: docs-registry-commands/when-a-command-is-interrupted-03
when-a-command-is-interrupted.text: --state-dir names the root of the journals, and the default is the per-user state directory. Recovering a registry command shows each of these interruptions on a development network.

where-the-keys-token-goes.name: docs-registry-commands/where-the-keys-token-goes-01
where-the-keys-token-goes.text: A registration commits, when it is booked, to the address that will hold its key's token once it is folded. open-datum insert commits the request address of open datum. The fold accepts any address a registration committed to, the address of the state validator itself included. A token folded into a holding at the state validator's own address stays where only the state validator can spend it. That is the choice of whoever booked the registration, and the fold does not refuse it.

conditions-the-figures-were-taken-under.name: docs-release-decision-table/conditions-the-figures-were-taken-under-00
conditions-the-figures-were-taken-under.text: Conditions the figures were taken under.

conditions-the-figures-were-taken-under.name: docs-release-decision-table/conditions-the-figures-were-taken-under-01
conditions-the-figures-were-taken-under.text: The creation receipts share one development network genesis and one set of protocol parameters, and the batch receipt carries the preprod parameters it evaluated under. The hashes below bind those inputs.

reading-the-decision-table.name: docs-release-decision-table/reading-the-decision-table-01
reading-the-decision-table.text: Each row is one measurement. The gain lists the figures that are lower than the alternative the row is compared with, and the regression lists those that are higher. Every compared figure is a cost, so lower is better. A figure that is equal is in neither list, and none measured means no compared figure was higher.

reading-the-decision-table.name: docs-release-decision-table/reading-the-decision-table-02
reading-the-decision-table.text: The batch rows rest on preprod protocol parameters recorded on Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:06:12 GMT, taken from the kept batch receipt. The creation rows rest on the development network's protocol parameters, read from its chain at the times the kept chain records note: 2026-10-29T04:25:37Z for both designs.

regenerate-this-page.name: docs-release-decision-table/regenerate-this-page-01
regenerate-this-page.text: Run python3 tools/decision_table.py --write to regenerate the page, then regenerate its speech and changed narration. The documentation check runs python3 tools/decision_table.py --check.

release-decision-table.name: docs-release-decision-table/release-decision-table-01
release-decision-table.text: As a reader deciding whether this release's measurements support your use, you find on this page the measurements this line delivered of what creating a registry costs and of the largest batch of requests one fold carries. Each row gives the conditions it was taken under, what it improved, what it made worse and what it did not measure.

release-decision-table.name: docs-release-decision-table/release-decision-table-02
release-decision-table.text: Every figure on the page is read or computed from the kept receipts below. The documentation check regenerates the page from the receipts and their chain records, and refuses a page that differs, a receipt or chain record that is missing and a row that names no receipt.

the-decision-table.name: docs-release-decision-table/the-decision-table-01
the-decision-table.text: The first two rows compare creating a registry under the previous design with the application-held design. The last three rows give the largest batch a fold carries, compared with a fold of one request.

the-decision-table.name: docs-release-decision-table/the-decision-table-02
the-decision-table.text: Creating a first registry takes 3 transactions under the application-held design against 5 under the previous design. What rose: registry-creating transaction bytes: 751 to 999; registry-creating transaction fee: 695626 to 1028555 lovelace. Creating a later registry takes 1 transaction under the application-held design against 4 under the previous design. What rose: registry-creating transaction bytes: 755 to 999; registry-creating transaction fee: 695371 to 1028555 lovelace.

the-decision-table.name: docs-release-decision-table/the-decision-table-03
the-decision-table.text: The largest accepted fold in the registrations workload carries 4 requests, and one more request exceeds the memory limit. Per request the largest batch costs less than a one-request fold in signed transaction bytes and fee and more in execution memory and execution steps. The largest accepted fold in the terminations workload carries 7 requests, and one more request exceeds the memory limit. Per request the largest batch costs less than a one-request fold in signed transaction bytes and fee and more in execution memory and execution steps. The largest accepted fold in the mixed workload carries 6 requests, and one more request exceeds the memory limit. Per request the largest batch costs less than a one-request fold in signed transaction bytes and fee and more in execution memory and execution steps.

the-kept-receipts.name: docs-release-decision-table/the-kept-receipts-01
the-kept-receipts.text: The receipts and the chain records they name are committed with the repository. Their SHA-256 is computed when this page is generated, so a file that changes also changes this page.

book-then-complete.name: docs-retirement/book-then-complete-01
book-then-complete.text: The booking command requires the holding's controller to sign. It donates the protected deposit and moves the active token into a pending request with one termination approval, no datum and the ADA available to reward its folder. The active token is not burned at booking.

book-then-complete.name: docs-retirement/book-then-complete-02
book-then-complete.text: The fold consumes the public request, burns its approval and active token, continues the registry with the terminal leaf and pays the request's whole held value to the folder. The folder pays the transaction fee and needs no file or signature from the controller. A termination cannot be reclaimed or cancelled, and the terminal key cannot be registered again.

book-then-complete.name: docs-retirement/book-then-complete-03
book-then-complete.text: Follow the termination commands for the flags, the pending output reference and the treasury donation reported by the booking receipt. Use the holding reference returned by your latest update.

permanently-terminate-a-key.name: docs-retirement/permanently-terminate-a-key-01
permanently-terminate-a-key.text: As a key's controller, you want to end its registration permanently. You first book a termination from its live holding. Any wallet can then complete it by folding the public request. The protected deposit goes to the treasury when you book, and the active token is burned when the request is folded.

refusals-and-evidence.name: docs-retirement/refusals-and-evidence-01
refusals-and-evidence.text: A missing holding, a different controller or another named registry is refused before signing. An unavailable provider answer remains unavailable; it does not establish absence or a ledger refusal.

refusals-and-evidence.name: docs-retirement/refusals-and-evidence-02
refusals-and-evidence.text: The consumer conformance record publishes the requirements and their evidence limits. A local builder check is not a connected ledger history. Demo 1 links the playable application journey and the release it runs.

create-another-registry-on-shared-public.name: docs-shared-publications/create-another-registry-on-shared-publications-00
create-another-registry-on-shared-public.text: Create another registry on shared publications.

create-another-registry-on-shared-public.name: docs-shared-publications/create-another-registry-on-shared-publications-01
create-another-registry-on-shared-public.text: As a registry creator, you can create your own registry using the live state and application scripts another wallet published for the same application release. You supply your own funded wallet, the release blueprint and provider settings. You need no file, key, registry state or publication address from that creator. Your registry has its own state token, configuration and root.

create-another-registry-on-shared-public.name: docs-shared-publications/create-another-registry-on-shared-publications-02
create-another-registry-on-shared-public.text: Install the commands and obtain the matching plutus.json from the verified release. The registry command guide describes booking, folding and recovery. The example below follows the development-network journey; its wallet keys are generated for that run. Use your own provider URL and network-time directory for the network your wallet uses.

create-another-registry-on-shared-public.name: docs-shared-publications/create-another-registry-on-shared-publications-03
create-another-registry-on-shared-public.text: The provider proposes live reference outputs. The command hashes the scripts those outputs actually carry before reusing them. Creation spends a fresh seed and reads the verified scripts by reference. A missing copy is published first. The new registry then uses the same booking and folding commands as the first registry.

create-with-your-own-wallet.name: docs-shared-publications/create-with-your-own-wallet-01
create-with-your-own-wallet.text: Erin's fresh working directory contains only her own key and the release blueprint. Her home and state directory contain no earlier creator's records. The journey runs this command with its generated provider settings:

create-with-your-own-wallet.name: docs-shared-publications/create-with-your-own-wallet-02
create-with-your-own-wallet.text: Keep the receipt's stateToken and registry address as public identifiers for your registry. When both copies remain live, submissions contains the creation alone; neither script entry reports a publication. If a copy has been spent or is absent, the command publishes only that missing copy before creating the registry.

read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.name: docs-shared-publications/read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receipt-00
read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.text: Read reuse and discovery from the receipt.

read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.name: docs-shared-publications/read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receipt-01
read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.text: Read these fields from your actual receipt:

read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.name: docs-shared-publications/read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receipt-02
read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.text: A foreign candidate stays visible even when another candidate is genuine and reused. If no genuine copy exists, the command skips foreign candidates and publishes the expected script. The provider's live-output query cannot distinguish a spent copy from one that never existed. An explicit reference location supplied to a command is still checked for a missing or mismatched script.

read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.name: docs-shared-publications/read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receipt-03
read-reuse-and-discovery-from-the-receip.text: Discovery here means lookup by script hash through your configured provider. A different application policy or release has a different applied state script and cannot reuse the earlier application's state copy. Publishing references for everyone and a general public discovery service remain outside this workflow. No witness-policy publication or witness-pin configuration is required.

read-the-measured-costs.name: docs-shared-publications/read-the-measured-costs-01
read-the-measured-costs.text: The creation-cost comparison is generated from the committed measurement receipts and checked against the included transaction bytes. Its table separates transaction fees from ADA locked in reference outputs. The later application-held creation reuses both scripts and creates no reference output; your own registry's state and configuration still lock their own ADA. Fees are measurements on the frozen development-network parameters, not a quote for another network or release.

read-the-measured-costs.name: docs-shared-publications/read-the-measured-costs-02
read-the-measured-costs.text: The candidate receipt contains first.totals and later.totals, with the transactions beneath each creation. From a repository checkout, read the measured figures directly:

read-the-measured-costs.name: docs-shared-publications/read-the-measured-costs-03
read-the-measured-costs.text: The carrying experiment records the actual sizes, evaluation and node outcomes of alternative creation forms. The shipped command keeps the shared-publication path.

recovery-and-evidence-limits.name: docs-shared-publications/recovery-and-evidence-limits-01
recovery-and-evidence-limits.text: After an interruption around publication, rerunning reuses every live copy and publishes only what is missing. An uncertain submission preserves its saved transaction identity and signed body; a later invocation reconciles it without automatically resubmitting it. Create is not idempotent: a further invocation can create another registry from a new seed. Repeating a spent explicit seed keeps the existing refusal. See command recovery.

recovery-and-evidence-limits.name: docs-shared-publications/recovery-and-evidence-limits-02
recovery-and-evidence-limits.text: Run the same packaged-command journey and retain its receipts:

recovery-and-evidence-limits.name: docs-shared-publications/recovery-and-evidence-limits-03
recovery-and-evidence-limits.text: The results directory must not already exist. It contains the creation receipts, discovery records, independent chain views, creation measurements, the shared-registration observation and its rejected controls, folder directory listings and a readable receipt. Throwaway wallet keys are removed when the run exits; partial diagnostics remain if a command fails.

recovery-and-evidence-limits.name: docs-shared-publications/recovery-and-evidence-limits-04
recovery-and-evidence-limits.text: The conformance inventory publishes the reuse requirements beside the existing requirements. Its runner computes their standings from receipts. These rows remain uncovered because no executable comparison with the application-held model exists yet. The registration journey, recovery partitions and measurement receipts are separate evidence boundaries and establish nothing about agreement with the model. An executable conformance language for creation claims is outside this change. Public discovery for everyone, batch limits and release acceptance remain separate work.

register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.name: docs-shared-publications/register-a-key-in-the-new-registry-00
register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.text: Register a key in the new registry.

register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.name: docs-shared-publications/register-a-key-in-the-new-registry-01
register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.text: Alice books a key, an initial payload and a deposit in Erin's registry. The journey supplies the new registry's public state token as state_token:

register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.name: docs-shared-publications/register-a-key-in-the-new-registry-02
register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.text: Bob starts a new working directory and home containing only his own key and the public release. He finds the pending registration through the chain provider, matching the registry identity and key. He supplies that public output reference as pending; Alice's payload file, key and command journal are not inputs:

register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.name: docs-shared-publications/register-a-key-in-the-new-registry-03
register-a-key-in-the-new-registry.text: The journey reads the included transactions independently: the fold consumes that registration's approval, burns it, mints the key's token into a holding carrying the booked payload and exact deposit, and spends and continues Erin's own state with a changed root. Altering the observation to name the first registry's state or to remove the holding's deposit fails the same check. The complete journey also checks that no transaction publishes a witness policy or adds a witness pin.

asking-the-program-for-help.name: docs-singular-node/asking-the-program-for-help-01
asking-the-program-for-help.text: As a registry operator, you can ask either program what it does before you read this page or any other. singular --version and open-datum --version print the program's name, its version and the commit it was built from; a build that carries no commit says commit unknown. singular --help and open-datum --help print one screen: what the program is for, and every command with a line about it. Each command has its own --help that shows only that command: its settings, each with a description and a default, the signer routes grouped with the vault first and the key file, which is legacy, last, the environment variables it reads, an example for a command that writes, and how it ends.

asking-the-program-for-help.name: docs-singular-node/asking-the-program-for-help-02
asking-the-program-for-help.text: A mistyped command or flag prints what is wrong in one line, the usage of the command you were heading for and where its help is, and exits with status 2. A mistyped command also names the nearest command. A failure that no command reported itself, such as a file that cannot be read, ends as one line on standard error saying what failed, with status 1, never the runtime's own report of an uncaught exception. Both programs complete commands and flags in your shell: source <(singular --bash-completion-script "$(which singular)") for bash, with --zsh-completion-script and --fish-completion-script for the other shells.

asking-the-program-for-help.name: docs-singular-node/asking-the-program-for-help-03
asking-the-program-for-help.text: The overview of each program follows, quoted from the program itself. The first line of every help page names the version and the commit; it is left out here, and VERSION stands for the version of the build. The documentation check runs the programs and fails when a quotation, or the settings table below, disagrees with what they print.

booking-and-folding.name: docs-singular-node/booking-and-folding-01
booking-and-folding.text: As a controller, use the registry command guide to book registrations, update holdings and book permanent termination. The fold takes explicit pending references and can be run by another wallet from public chain inputs. Its command is open-datum fold.

choosing-a-registrys-windows.name: docs-singular-node/choosing-a-registrys-windows-01
choosing-a-registrys-windows.text: Use open-datum create --process-time MS --reclaim-time MS to choose the processing and reclaim windows once. The guide describes their defaults and the booking-width parameter.

connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.name: docs-singular-node/connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider-00
connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.text: Connecting singular to a ledger provider.

connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.name: docs-singular-node/connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider-01
connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.text: Dated qualification, 2026-10-15: rejection after the window, rejection before the deadline, request value and refund routing, rejection and retraction refund controls, and rejection inside the processing and retraction windows are all unmet by ruling: implementation follows the superseded rule; the ruled rule is not implemented. The live comparisons still exercise the legacy rejection that spends the registry state output. The ruled rejection reads that output by reference and never spends it. Agreement with the legacy path is not acceptance of the ruled design. The earlier processing-window consumer requirement and the unresolved refund-routing requirement remain open. Historical results below retain their original revision and evidence binding; they do not establish current acceptance.

connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.name: docs-singular-node/connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider-02
connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.text: As a registry operator, you create a registry through singular registry create and sign and submit bundles through singular wallet and singular submit. You create, insert, fold, update, terminate, reclaim and clean up through open-datum, with a Koios API on your chosen network. The commands that create a registry and book, fold, reclaim and clean up a registration are described in create a registry and register keys on the proved design. You supply the API settings and pinned time material; each write is signed from your vault, or by a signer elsewhere through a bundle file (see Signing a write elsewhere, or from your vault). Commands read raw facts through one logical session, build and evaluate locally, submit signed transactions, and preserve recovery evidence in the registry journal.

connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.name: docs-singular-node/connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider-03
connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.text: Words such as registry, state token, request, fold, window, vault and bundle are explained as they first appear in the step-by-step page of singular-demo; the Demo 1 page tells the story in short.

connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.name: docs-singular-node/connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider-04
connecting-singular-to-a-ledger-provider.text: The ordinary provider is Koios. Old backend and socket settings are refused before acquisition or registry effects. The current provider session promises no coherent chain snapshot and carries no verification witness.

following-what-a-command-does.name: docs-singular-node/following-what-a-command-does-01
following-what-a-command-does.text: As a registry operator, you can watch a command's progress while it runs and keep its typed event stream as data. The retained commands emit command and transaction events. Protocol-fact narration is unavailable on these commands. Standard output carries only the result: inspect prints human text unless --json is selected, and writes print JSON receipts. Narration does not change either result.

following-what-a-command-does.name: docs-singular-node/following-what-a-command-does-02
following-what-a-command-does.text: On a terminal a command narrates what to standard error unless told otherwise.

following-what-a-command-does.name: docs-singular-node/following-what-a-command-does-03
following-what-a-command-does.text: Indentation reflects the event's scope. Transaction mechanics retain their identifiers and elapsed times. A failure says where it happened, and the four places are distinct: refused by the client before anything was submitted, refused by local script evaluation before anything was submitted, rejected by the ledger, or refused by the provider, so that no ledger judged the transaction.

following-what-a-command-does.name: docs-singular-node/following-what-a-command-does-04
following-what-a-command-does.text: With --trace-format json, or a file:PATH sink, each event is one JSON object on its own line, written as it happens: its level (what or how), its scope (outermost first) and its event with that event's fields, in full. The last line of every stream is command-ended, naming the command, the outcome class of its receipt and its elapsed time. No event carries a signing key or the text of a failure: a failure names only its type.

following-what-a-command-does.name: docs-singular-node/following-what-a-command-does-05
following-what-a-command-does.text: A sink that cannot be written, a closed standard error or a full disk loses that sink's narration and nothing else: the other sinks, the receipt, the journal and the exit status are as they would be with no narration at all.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-00
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: Giving the chain, the contracts and the registry once.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-01
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: As a registry operator, you type the same six settings on nearly every command: the Koios address, the network magic and the pinned time directory (the chain), the blueprint (the compiled contracts), and the state directory and the state token, or the registry's address, which holds the state token and the network (the registry). You can write them once. Each has three forms, and the first one that is present wins.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-02
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: The variable is SINGULAR_ followed by the flag's name in capitals with underscores, and the key is the flag's name without its dashes. The six above are --koios-url, --network-time, --network-magic, --blueprint, --state-dir and --state-token. Six more have the same three forms: --registry, --koios-token-file, the narration controls --trace, --trace-to and --trace-format, and --vault. The --help of every command lists the three forms of each of them that the command takes, and says where the config file is.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-03
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: The config file is one JSON object. Both programs read the same file: it is singular.json in the folder you run the command from, or the file named by --config FILE or by the variable SINGULAR_CONFIG. With a file like this in your demo folder, open-datum insert --key alice --payload payload.json --vault alice.vault is a whole command, and it does exactly what the same command with the six flags does:

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-04
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: What you see when something is wrong:

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-05
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: A missing setting is refused in the usual line, missing --koios-url, and below it one line names the flag, the variable and the key that would give it.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-06
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: A file that does not exist when you named it, that is not JSON, that is not one object, or that holds a key the program does not read is refused in one sentence naming the file. A key that is nearly a setting's name says which one it nearly is. A default singular.json that is not there is no file; one that is there and broken is refused. A problem with the file never stops --help or --version.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-07
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: A path in the file means what the same path means on the command line: it is read from the folder the command runs from.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-08
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: A value is text or a number, as network-magic above; an empty text or null is no setting.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-09
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: Nothing else can come from the file or the environment. The key file, an external signer, the passphrase and what a command does stay on the command line: a file that names a passphrase is refused, and the passphrase stays on the terminal prompt or on the descriptor --passphrase-fd names. The environment gives a passphrase only on a development network, as SINGULAR_PASSPHRASE; the section after the vault one says how.

giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.name: docs-singular-node/giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-registry-once-10
giving-the-chain-the-contracts-and-the-r.text: A line that carries every flag it needs means what it meant before. An environment variable or a file only fills in what the line leaves out, so a flag you type is never overruled.

harness-appendix-test-hooks.name: docs-singular-node/harness-appendix-test-hooks-01
harness-appendix-test-hooks.text: Released singular and open-datum binaries carry no fault-injection or hidden trie-diagnostic hooks.

how-long-a-bundle-can-wait.name: docs-singular-node/how-long-a-bundle-can-wait-00
how-long-a-bundle-can-wait.text: How long a bundle can wait.

how-long-a-bundle-can-wait.name: docs-singular-node/how-long-a-bundle-can-wait-01
how-long-a-bundle-can-wait.text: The recovery guide describes unresolved submissions. No automatic resubmission follows an interrupted or uncertain send.

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.name: docs-singular-node/keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted-vault-00
keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: Keeping your signing key in an encrypted vault.

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.name: docs-singular-node/keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted-vault-01
keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: As Alice, I keep my payment signing key in one encrypted file instead of a plaintext key on disk. I run singular wallet create naming a new vault and a network, type a passphrase twice, and see my address on one line:

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.name: docs-singular-node/keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted-vault-02
keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: My key exists only inside that file: nothing else is written, no public part is kept beside it, and reading my address later means opening the vault — the same address prints, from the same passphrase:

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.name: docs-singular-node/keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted-vault-03
keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: A script supplies the passphrase on an inherited file descriptor, one line, and is never asked for a confirmation:

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.name: docs-singular-node/keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted-vault-04
keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: On a development network a script can set SINGULAR_PASSPHRASE instead, which a descriptor outranks; preprod and the other public networks refuse the variable (see the passphrase from the environment).

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.name: docs-singular-node/keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted-vault-05
keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: Creating over an existing path — a symbolic link included — is refused before a passphrase is asked for, with that path's bytes untouched; wallet address on a vault that is not there or cannot be read says so in one sentence naming the file, also before it asks for a passphrase; the vault file is made readable by its owner only, and a write that fails removes the file it made. A wrong passphrase, a corrupt file and a file that is not a vault all answer one refusal naming no secret, nothing prints on standard output, and the empty passphrase is refused at birth. Every creation draws a fresh key from the operating system's entropy: fresh entropy for every vault.

keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.name: docs-singular-node/keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted-vault-06
keeping-your-signing-key-in-an-encrypted.text: The vault is an ordinary age file, one passphrase recipient with scrypt work factor 18, holding the key's standard text envelope as its plaintext. Any age tool opens it with the passphrase and yields the envelope: age --decrypt alice.vault asks for the passphrase on the terminal and prints the plaintext, and the decrypted bytes are the cardano-cli key format itself, accepted wherever a signing-key file is read.

naming-the-registry.name: docs-singular-node/naming-the-registry-01
naming-the-registry.text: Use the state token or the registry address printed by creation. The registry command guide describes the retained forms.

public-environment-configuration.name: docs-singular-node/public-environment-configuration-01
public-environment-configuration.text: As an operator, I can supply each setting of the section above as a variable, for example SINGULAR_STATE_TOKEN when I omit --state-token; an explicit command-line value takes precedence, and the config file comes after the variable. The token names the registry, and never selects a provider. SINGULAR_CONFIG names the config file. SINGULAR_LOG=PATH appends phase events to a file alongside the narration sinks selected by --trace, --trace-to and --trace-format. It does not replace those sinks or change their command-line precedence. An empty phase-log path disables that sink.

reading-a-key.name: docs-singular-node/reading-a-key-01
reading-a-key.text: As a reader, give the registry address and a key to learn its status and application without a signing key, a blueprint or a local registry directory:

reading-a-key.name: docs-singular-node/reading-a-key-02
reading-a-key.text: The address supplies the network and the state token. Give it as --registry, SINGULAR_REGISTRY, or the registry key of the settings file, in that order of precedence. The provider URL follows the same flag, environment, file order. The established --state-token with --network-magic spelling also works; settings beside an address must agree with it. Use --key-hex for binary keys.

reading-a-key.name: docs-singular-node/reading-a-key-03
reading-a-key.text: The neutral command answers active, terminal, never-registered, unavailable or refused. Its application identity contains the policy, script and known releases from the packaged release table; an empty release list means not released yet. For active custody, datum is the exact detailed Plutus data, datumKind distinguishes inline, hash and none, and a hash is printed as datumHash. The command interprets no application envelope.

reading-a-key.name: docs-singular-node/reading-a-key-04
reading-a-key.text: The application command refines active into live, with control, deposit in lovelace, payload and payloadSchema, or pending-termination. It retains every neutral refusal and state-backed absence. The full live datum remains under envelope; see what inspect prints.

reading-a-key.name: docs-singular-node/reading-a-key-05
reading-a-key.text: A live read uses exactly one active-asset lookup after checking the provider's network. A missing active token alone proves nothing: terminal and never registered require the recognised registry state and its authenticated trie leaf, reconstructed from public history. Unknown policies, wrong networks, conflicting tokens and tokens outside application custody are refused. Failed or incomplete reads stay unavailable, with their reason.

reading-a-key.name: docs-singular-node/reading-a-key-06
reading-a-key.text: Both commands print human text by default. --json prints one object for a script. Exit status 0 means an answer, including terminal and never registered; 1 means unavailable; 2 means refused evidence or an invalid command line. Neither command accepts signing settings.

reading-a-key.name: docs-singular-node/reading-a-key-07
reading-a-key.text: --query-work adds calls, rows and response bytes for each provider read and the total. JSON carries them in queryWork.reads and queryWork.total; human text shows the same counts. Measurements include each transport page and exclude provider startup and other sessions. When measured trace evidence is missing, queryWork.unavailable explains that limit instead of inventing zero work. These counts describe this read, not a coherent chain snapshot.

reading-through-an-index.name: docs-singular-node/reading-through-an-index-01
reading-through-an-index.text: The former --backend node / --backend indexer comparison is retired. Ordinary commands use the Koios path only. They do not create an in-memory chain index or accept an ordinary node socket: the production node read adapter and the in-memory indexer are removed with the provider migration, and no registry command names a node backend. Private generated nodes and independent LSQ probes remain test harness components behind the private facade; none of them ships with the terminal.

reading-through-an-index.name: docs-singular-node/reading-through-an-index-02
reading-through-an-index.text: An index must not fabricate transaction history for genesis-only allocations. The retained private genesis-only control uses genuine initial ledger outputs and refuses coverage-incomplete, naming their output references, with exit 12 and no registry write. Funding those allocations through a real transaction creates full-block history that the accepting control can read. This is a private source control, not a promise that every remote service detects all missing history. Missing or inconsistent registry reconstruction remains a refusal and must not become an empty registry.

signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.name: docs-singular-node/signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transactions-offline-00
signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.text: Signing a bundle of unsigned transactions offline.

signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.name: docs-singular-node/signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transactions-offline-01
signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.text: As Bob, I receive a bundle of unsigned transactions from a writer — one JSON file — and I run singular wallet sign on an offline machine, naming my vault and the bundle. I type my passphrase once and get one witness file per transaction, with the paths on standard output and a short summary of what I signed on standard error:

signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.name: docs-singular-node/signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transactions-offline-02
signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.text: The writer's side is a singular registry create run, or an open-datum create, insert, update, terminate or fold run, that names --wallet-address and --bundle in place of the signing key: it builds its whole run as one bundle in build order, signs and sends nothing, states its own fields under expected in its receipt, and exits with status 19, waiting-for-signatures.

signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.name: docs-singular-node/signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transactions-offline-03
signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.text: The bundle names the network it is built for, so no network setting is taken: every provider and registry option is refused by name, and the command opens no connection — it reads nothing but the bundle file, the vault file and the passphrase. A bundle is refused by name, and nothing is written, when a recorded identity is not the hash of its transaction's body, a recorded deadline is not the body's validity upper bound, an identity names two transactions, a key hash a body requires is covered by no signer address, or the vault's own address is not among the signers. A witness file that already exists is refused with its bytes untouched.

signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.name: docs-singular-node/signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transactions-offline-04
signing-a-bundle-of-unsigned-transaction.text: Each witness is the standard TxWitness ConwayEra text envelope of one verification-key witness — my public key and my signature over that transaction's own hash — so the submitting command (or any Cardano tool) can check and assemble them. The effects lines a bundle carries are the writer's claims: the summary shows them, and nothing trusts them. The registry a bundle names is the writer's statement too: the summary says so beside the name, and singular submit is where the bundle meets the chain. Whether the signers list is complete cannot be checked offline — inputs cannot be resolved — and expiry is not judged without a clock that knows the slot; both are the submitting command's judgement. No output, refusal or file names the passphrase or any key byte.

signing-a-write-elsewhere-or-from-your-v.name: docs-singular-node/signing-a-write-elsewhere-or-from-your-vault-00
signing-a-write-elsewhere-or-from-your-v.text: Signing a write elsewhere, or from your vault.

signing-a-write-elsewhere-or-from-your-v.name: docs-singular-node/signing-a-write-elsewhere-or-from-your-vault-01
signing-a-write-elsewhere-or-from-your-v.text: Use --vault FILE for a local vault, or --wallet-address ADDR --bundle FILE for an external signer. The retained writers use the same signer options. See offline signing and submission.

submitting-a-signed-bundle.name: docs-singular-node/submitting-a-signed-bundle-01
submitting-a-signed-bundle.text: As Bob, I hand back the witnesses for a bundle and run singular submit with the node settings. The transactions are sent in the bundle's order, and the receipt says what the chain shows. If the run is cut short, I run the same command again: it sends only the transactions the chain does not hold yet. If a body has expired, it says to rebuild the bundle and sends nothing. It needs no wallet key and keeps no state.

submitting-a-signed-bundle.name: docs-singular-node/submitting-a-signed-bundle-02
submitting-a-signed-bundle.text: Bundles from the application commands need no registry name and no release to submit. An optional registry name remains the writer's statement; it is checked for state-token syntax, and does not establish what the transactions act on. Transaction identities, required signatures, resolved inputs and the chain's readback determine submission and its receipt.

submitting-a-signed-bundle.name: docs-singular-node/submitting-a-signed-bundle-03
submitting-a-signed-bundle.text: The witness files are the ones singular wallet sign writes; a directory stands for the .witness files it holds, and each witness is matched to a transaction by its signature, never by its file name. The command checks everything it can before it sends anything, in this order. Without touching the chain, it refuses a bundle the signing step would refuse, an optional registry name that is not a state token, a witness file it cannot read, and a witness whose signature verifies against no transaction of the bundle. Then it reads the chain once: where each transaction sits, the tip, and the inputs of each transaction not on chain yet — an input an earlier transaction of the bundle produces is taken from that transaction, every other from the chain. Witnesses are required for the transactions this run will send, and for those alone. It refuses a witness for a key none of them needs, a transaction left without a witness for a key it needs (its required signers and the payment keys of what it spends), an input found nowhere, and a transaction not on chain whose validity upper bound the tip has reached, with the word rebuild. A refusal exits as a client refusal, naming its cause, with an empty list of submissions.

submitting-a-signed-bundle.name: docs-singular-node/submitting-a-signed-bundle-04
submitting-a-signed-bundle.text: A transaction the chain already holds, found by its identity, is skipped before those checks, and the witnesses supplied for it are ignored: the inputs it spent can no longer be read from the chain, and it is never sent again. A witness that cannot be read, or that verifies against no transaction of the bundle, is refused all the same, before the chain is read, even when every transaction is already on chain.

submitting-a-signed-bundle.name: docs-singular-node/submitting-a-signed-bundle-05
submitting-a-signed-bundle.text: Each transaction the chain does not hold is sent in turn, carrying exactly its own witnesses, and confirmed before the next. An answer that may or may not mean the node took the transaction stops the run as partial, and nothing is sent again within the run; the next run finds what landed. Once every transaction is on chain, the receipt is read back from the chain: for each transaction, whether this run sent it or found it, its chain point, its confirmations, and each of its outputs — unspent with what it holds, or spent since — plus the bundle's hash.

submitting-a-signed-bundle.name: docs-singular-node/submitting-a-signed-bundle-06
submitting-a-signed-bundle.text: The effect lines a bundle carries are its writer's claims: the receipt shows them under claims and never says they were confirmed. The completeness of the signatures is judged here, against the inputs the chain resolves, which the offline signing step cannot do. Expiry is judged against the tip read before the first send. A command that stops leaves nothing behind but its receipt, and it never resubmits on its own. A valid signature by an unneeded key over an already-landed body is not reported.

the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.name: docs-singular-node/the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a-development-network-00
the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.text: The passphrase from the environment on a development network.

the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.name: docs-singular-node/the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a-development-network-01
the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.text: As a reader of the tutorial on a private development network, I sign with a deliberately weak passphrase and do not want to type it at every command. I export it once, and every command that opens a vault reads it, with the other settings given as the sections above describe:

the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.name: docs-singular-node/the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a-development-network-02
the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.text: wallet create takes the variable for both of its asks, so a creation is not asked to confirm. A development network is any network that is not one of the three public ones the build names: mainnet (network magic 764824073), preprod (1) and preview (2). On those three, a command that would read the variable is refused in one sentence that names the variable and the network, before the vault is read. The sentence is the line a wallet command prints on standard error and the reason in the receipt of a write that was refused by the client:

the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.name: docs-singular-node/the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a-development-network-03
the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.text: The decision uses the network magic the command already receives. wallet sign is offline and takes no network magic, so it uses the network the bundle names, once it has read the bundle and before it reads the vault. A write is refused on mainnet before any passphrase is considered, so for a write the variable is refused on preprod and preview.

the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.name: docs-singular-node/the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a-development-network-04
the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.text: The variable is the whole of this: there is no config key for it and no flag, and a config file that names a passphrase is refused. The descriptor wins: with --passphrase-fd N on the command the variable is not read, on any network. With neither, the prompt is as before. A variable that is set but empty is refused, naming the variable, rather than taken as an empty passphrase.

the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.name: docs-singular-node/the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a-development-network-05
the-passphrase-from-the-environment-on-a.text: The variable is for a passphrase that protects nothing. Every process you start inherits your environment, and a process of your account can read it, so a real vault keeps the prompt or the descriptor.

the-settings-you-give.name: docs-singular-node/the-settings-you-give-01
the-settings-you-give.text: The URL, network magic and one signer (a key file, a vault, or an address with its bundle file) travel together on a write: naming only some of them is refused as partially configured, and so is a write that names none, because singular never starts a node of its own — a registry booted on a chain that dies with the process could not be attached to again. The refusal says which part is missing and, for the signer, the three ways to name one: the vault first, then an address with its bundle file, and last the key file, which is legacy. The settings that do not change from one command to the next (the node, the contracts, the registry, the token file, the narration and the vault) can be given once, as the next section says; the key file, an external signer and everything else a command does are typed on the command. Public environment configuration lists the variables and the phase-log path.

the-settings-you-give.name: docs-singular-node/the-settings-you-give-02
the-settings-you-give.text: The file alice.json is the key's payload, ordinary JSON stored as plain JSON unless --payload-schema detailed says it is written in the detailed Plutus data schema; store ordinary JSON as a key's payload gives the rules.

the-settings-you-give.name: docs-singular-node/the-settings-you-give-03
the-settings-you-give.text: An automatic fold skips each individually unfoldable request with its reason: an already registered key, an inactive termination key, a deposit below the holding's minimum or a closed processing window. The first individually foldable request for a key in take order is kept; later foldable requests for it are skipped as duplicates. The receipt lists every skip, and left counts only foldable requests outside the selected prefix. If none can fold, the command refuses with nothing to fold and retains the skip list. Explicit --pending batches keep their existing refusals and are never shortened.

the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.name: docs-singular-node/the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-file-00
the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.text: The vault from the environment or the file.

the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.name: docs-singular-node/the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-file-01
the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.text: As an operator who signs with a vault, you can name it once: SINGULAR_VAULT=alice.vault, or "vault": "alice.vault" in the config file, and open-datum insert --key alice --payload payload.json signs from it. The passphrase is not part of this: it stays on the terminal prompt, or on the descriptor --passphrase-fd names on the command, with a vault from either source just as with a typed one. A development network can also take it from the environment, as the next section says.

the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.name: docs-singular-node/the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-file-02
the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.text: A write is signed by exactly one signer, so a vault you did not type on the command never joins another signer you did. If the line names the key file --wallet-skey, or an external signer with --wallet-address or --bundle, the command is refused in one sentence that names where the vault comes from and the flag on the line, before anything is read or sent:

the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.name: docs-singular-node/the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-file-03
the-vault-from-the-environment-or-the-fi.text: For a vault from the file, the sentence names the key and the file (the "vault" key of singular.json) and says to remove the key. The wallet commands wallet create, wallet address and wallet sign take the vault from either source too: wallet create still refuses a path that is taken before it asks for a passphrase.

what-a-write-records.name: docs-singular-node/what-a-write-records-01
what-a-write-records.text: The recovery guide describes the retained commands' journals, transaction identities and refusal to resubmit an uncertain transaction.

what-each-receipt-says.name: docs-singular-node/what-each-receipt-says-01
what-each-receipt-says.text: The registry command guide describes the receipt for each retained operation.
